"I went to my room and found the dress as he had said. It was
of a peculiar shade of blue, and though it had evidently been
worn, it fitted me as if it had been made for me. When I
returned to the drawing-room, I found Mr. Rucastle and his wife
sitting in the window, and they both expressed the greatest
satisfaction at my appearance. Mr. Rucastle then placed a chair
for me in such a way that my back was to the window, and he
began to tell me the most comical stories, which made me laugh
until I was quite exhausted. Mrs. Rucastle, however, sat
perfectly still, with her hands in her lap, and never even
smiled. I could see that she was watching me with a very
strange expression, as if she were trying to find some
resemblance which she expected to see there."

"The dress which I found waiting for me was of a peculiar shade
of blue. It was of excellent material, a sort of beige, but it
bore unmistakable signs of having been worn before. It could not
have been a better fit if I had been measured for it. Both Mr.
and Mrs. Rucastle expressed a delight at the look of it, which
seemed quite exaggerated in its vehemence. They were waiting for
me in the drawing-room, which is a very large room, stretching
along the entire front of the house, with three long windows
reaching down to the floor. A chair had been placed close to the
central window, with its back turned towards it. In this I was
asked to sit, and then Mr. Rucastle, walking up and down on the
other side of the room, began to tell me a series of the funniest
stories that I have ever listened to. You cannot imagine how
comical he was, and I laughed until I was quite weary. Mrs.
Rucastle, however, who has evidently no sense of humour, never so
much as smiled, but sat with her hands in her lap, and a sad,
anxious look upon her face. After an hour or so, Mr. Rucastle
suddenly remarked that it was time to commence the duties of the
day, and that I might change my dress and go to little Edward in
the nursery.

"You can imagine, Mr. Holmes, that my curiosity was now thoroughly aroused. Why should I be made to sit in that particular chair, with my back to the window? It was evident that I was intended to be seen, but not to see. I determined to find out what it was that lay behind me. On the next occasion, I took a small mirror with me, concealed in my handkerchief. By tilting it carefully while I pretended to be engrossed in my book, I obtained a clear view of the road. There, leaning against the railings of the plantation, was a man. He was a youngish man, well-dressed, and he was staring up at the window with an expression of the most intense interest. The moment I made a slight movement he drew back into the shadow of the trees. It was clear that I was being used as a lure for this person, though for what possible reason I could not imagine."

"You can imagine, Mr. Holmes, that my curiosity was excited by
these extraordinary performances. I observed that they were
always very careful to keep my back to the window, and I began to
have a great desire to know what was going on behind me. At
first it seemed impossible, but I soon devised a means. I had a
small bit of broken looking-glass which I had used for my toilet,
and I managed to pin this into my handkerchief in such a way that
by holding it at an angle I could see what was happening in the
road behind me. I did this the next time that I was called upon
to sit in the window. I had to be very careful, for Mr. Rucastle
is as quick as a bird, but I managed it at last. I saw that there
was a man standing upon the Southampton road, a small,
bearded man in a grey suit, who was looking up at the house. He
was looking, not at me, but at the window in which I sat. I could
see by the way in which he waved his hand that he was trying to
communicate with someone, but whether it was with me or with
someone else in the house I could not say. The moment that I made
the discovery, Mr. Rucastle, whose eyes were never off my face,
must have guessed that I had seen something, for he suddenly
changed his manner and ordered me to leave the room and to take
off the dress."

"You can easily imagine, Mr. Holmes, how my curiosity was excited
by these very peculiar antics. I began to ask myself what they
could possibly mean. I noticed that I was always placed with my
back to the window, and I also noticed that they were very
careful that I should never turn my head. At last a device
occurred to me. I had a small hand-mirror in my pocket, and next
day, when the funny stories were in full swing, I managed to hold
it up so that I could see what was behind me. I had only a
glimpse, but it was enough. There was a man standing on the
highroad, a tall, bearded man in a grey suit, who was looking up
intently at the window where I sat. He was not looking at me,
but at the window itself. Next moment Mrs. Rucastle, who seemed to
have eyes at the back of her head, saw what I was doing. She gave
a little cry, and her husband's manner changed in an instant. He
was no longer the jovial companion, but a man with a hard, cruel
face and eyes which glared at me with fury. He told me that there
was a person on the road who was an enemy of his, and that he had
used me to make that person believe that his daughter Alice was
still at home. He warned me that if I ever looked out of the
window again, I should be sent away at once."

"You can easily imagine, Mr. Holmes, how my curiosity was excited by these very extraordinary proceedings. I was eager to know what lay behind me as I sat with my back to the window, and why I was so carefully forbidden to turn my head. At first, it seemed a mere caprice, but the repetition of the act and the care with which I was placed suggested a deeper motive. I bethought me of a small fragment of a mirror which I had in my work-basket, and on the next occasion, while laughing heartily at one of Mr. Rucastle’s jokes, I managed to hold it in such a way that I could see what was happening in the road behind me."

"You can easily imagine, Mr. Holmes, how my curiosity to know what
could be the object of this strange farce began to master me. I
could not help observing that they were both very anxious that I
should sit just so, and that they were also very careful that I
should never turn my head to look out of the window. At last I
devised a means of seeing what was behind me without appearing to
do so. I had a small piece of a broken mirror in my pocket, and
one day, by placing it in my handkerchief and adjusting it in my
hand, I was able to see the road behind me. I had hardly done so
before I saw that there was a man there, a young man in a grey
suit, who was standing on the footpath and looking up at me with
the greatest interest. He was looking at me, or rather at the
window, and I was convinced that it was for his benefit that this
extraordinary performance was being enacted."

"You can easily imagine, Mr. Holmes, how curious I became as to
what the meaning of this extraordinary performance could possibly
be. They were always very careful, I observed, to turn my face
away from the window, so that I became consumed with the desire
to see what was going on behind my back. At first it seemed to be
impossible, but I soon devised a means. My hand-mirror had been
broken, so a happy thought seized me, and I concealed a piece of
the glass in my handkerchief. On the next occasion, in the midst
of my laughter, I put my handkerchief up to my eyes, and was able
with a little management to see all that there was behind me. I
confess that I was disappointed. There was nothing. At least that
was my first impression. At the second glance, however, I
perceived that there was a man standing in the Southampton Road,
a small bearded man in a grey suit, who seemed to be looking in
my direction. The road is an important highway, and there are
usually people there. This man, however, was leaning against the
railings which bordered our field and was looking earnestly up. I
lowered my handkerchief and glanced at Mrs. Rucastle to find her
eyes fixed upon me with a most searching gaze. She said nothing,
but I am convinced that she had divined that I had a mirror in my
hand and had seen what was behind me. She rose at once.

"'Jephro,' said she, 'there is an impertinent fellow upon the
road there who stares up at Miss Hunter.'

"'No friend of yours, Miss Hunter?' he asked.

"'No, I know no one in these parts.'

"'Dear me! How very impertinent! Kindly turn round and motion to
him to go away.'

"'Surely it would be better to take no notice.'

"'No, no, we should have him loitering here always. Kindly turn
round and wave him away like that.'

"I must tell you now of another matter," she continued, "which
has perhaps more than anything else contributed to my feeling
of unease. There is a wing of the house, at the end of the
corridor in which my own room is situated, which appears to be
entirely uninhabited. The door which leads to it is always
locked, and I have never seen anyone enter it, save Mr.
Rucastle himself. He goes there once or twice a day, and I
have noticed that he carries a key upon his watch-chain. One
afternoon, however, as I was passing, I found that he had
omitted to turn the bolt, and that the door was standing ajar.
I could not resist the impulse to look in."

"It was not only the hair, however, which preyed upon my mind," she continued, her brow furrowing with the memory. "There is a certain wing of the house, situated at the rear, which appears to be entirely isolated from the rest. The windows are not only shuttered but are further secured by iron bars, and the heavy door which leads to the passage is invariably locked. On one occasion, I surprised Mr. Rucastle coming from this direction; he was carrying a large tray, and his usual jovial expression had been replaced by a look of such concentrated malice that I shrank back into the shadows to avoid him. It is my conviction, Mr. Holmes, that someone is being held captive in that wing, and that my presence in the house is in some way connected to the concealment of this prisoner."

You will understand, Mr. Holmes, that my curiosity was now fully aroused. I felt that I was moving in the midst of some strange conspiracy, the threads of which I could not grasp. A few days after the incident of the window, I happened to discover a locked drawer in the bureau of my bedroom. The key had been left in the lock, and upon opening it, I found a long, heavy tress of hair, of a very peculiar shade of chestnut—the very same shade, Mr. Holmes, as my own. I held it up to the light, and I tell you that it was identical in every respect. I was still shivering at the sight of it when I heard a footstep in the corridor, and I had just time to thrust it back and close the drawer before Mrs. Rucastle entered the room. She said nothing, but her eyes fixed themselves upon the drawer with a look of such intense suspicion that I felt certain she knew I had been prying.

It was on that same evening that I made a discovery which added a new element of mystery to my situation. While arranging my belongings in the heavy, old-fashioned bureau which stood in my room, I found that one of the top drawers was locked. A little searching among some old keys in a trinket-box provided me with one that served the purpose. Within, I found a coil of hair, wrapped in a piece of tissue paper. When I unfolded it, I could not suppress a cry of astonishment. It was a long, thick tress of a peculiar chestnut shade—the exact shade, Mr. Holmes, of the hair which I had so recently sacrificed at the command of my employer. I compared it with the few strands that remained to me, and I tell you that they were indistinguishable.

"You will find it difficult to believe the next discovery which I made," Miss Hunter continued. "I was rummaging in a drawer of a bureau in my room—a piece of furniture which was unlocked, though it contained nothing of value—when I came upon a small coil of hair, tied with a bit of ribbon. When I took it to the window and examined it, I was amazed to see that it was of the same peculiar chestnut tint as my own. I was still pondering this when I noticed another strange circumstance. There is one wing of the house which appears to be entirely uninhabited, and the door leading to it is always locked. One day, however, as I passed, I saw Mr. Rucastle emerge from this door, looking remarkably flustered, and he immediately locked it behind him with a large key which he thrust into his pocket. His face, usually so jovial, was set in lines of grim determination that I had never seen before."

"You will find it rather disconnected, I fear, and there may
prove to be little relation between the different incidents of
which I speak. On the very first day that I was at the Copper
Beeches, Mr. Rucastle took me to a small outhouse which stands
near the kitchen door. As we approached it I heard the sharp
rattling of a chain, and the sound as of a large animal moving
about.

"'Look in here!' said Mr. Rucastle, showing me a slit between two
planks. 'Is he not a beauty?'

"I looked through and was conscious of two glowing eyes, and of a
vague figure huddled up in the darkness.

"The warning was no idle one, for on the very next night I happened to look out of my bedroom window, and there, in the moonlight, I saw a large, shadowy form prowling about the lawn, and heard the low, deep growl which told of the presence of the brute. But there was another thing which puzzled me even more than the dog or the man in the road. I have told you that my own hair had been cut short. One day, while rummaging in the bottom of an old chest of drawers in my room, I came upon a coil of hair, wrapped in a piece of tissue paper. It was of the same peculiar tint as my own, and, as far as I could judge, of the same length and thickness. I was still holding it in my hand and wondering how it could have come there when Mrs. Rucastle entered the room. She looked at me with those cold, grey eyes of hers, and I saw her face turn even paler than its wont."

"The warning was no idle one, for two nights later I happened to
look out of my bedroom window about two o'clock in the morning.
It was a beautiful moonlight night, and the lawn in front of the
house was as bright as day. I was amazed to see a terrific brute
as big as a young calf, which was very slowly passing across the
grass. As I watched it, it raised its head and looked up at my
window with its bloodshot eyes and its slavering hanging jowl. I
confess that I could not help shivering with a terror which the
stoutest-hearted man might feel. I was grateful for the bars
which I noticed for the first time were across my lower windows.
In fact, the whole of that wing in which I live is barred in that
fashion. It would be impossible for any one to get out at night,
and it would be equally impossible for any one to get in.

"And now I come to the most incomprehensible part of my story."

"The warning was no idle one, for two nights later I happened to
look out of my bedroom window about two o'clock in the morning.
It was a beautiful moonlight night, and the lawn in front of the
house was as bright as day. I was amazed to see a terrific brute
as big as a young calf, which was prowling slowly across the
grass. As I watched it, it came up to the edge of the copper
beeches and stood for some time looking up at my window. I shall
never forget the glint of its eyes and the sharp white of its
venomous-looking teeth. It was a most hideous object. I
confessed I was more than ever thankful that I had been forewarned
against going out after dark.

"I have another little incident to bring to your notice, and
this, in its way, is even more strange than the other. You know
that my hair has been cut in a very peculiar way, and I thought
that I had left all the trimmings in my bedroom in London. I was
surprised one day, when searching for something else in the
bottom of my trunk, to come upon a large coil of hair, of
exactly the same shade and texture as my own. It was a most
extraordinary thing, and I was unable to account for it, but I
could not help thinking that it had some connection with the
strange conditions under which I had been engaged."

"This is very interesting," said Holmes, "and what was the next
occurrence?"

"The warning was no idle one, for two nights later I happened to
look out of my bedroom window about two o'clock in the morning.
It was a beautiful moonlight night, and the lawn in front of the
house was as bright as day. I was amazed to see a huge dog as
large as a calf, tawny-coloured, with hanging jowl, hanging
pendant from his huge white throat. He was walking slowly across
the lawn and settled down in front of the main door. He looked
more like some wild beast than a dog, and I could well understand
the safety with which the Rucastles could sleep with such a
guardian outside their shutters.

"And now I have a very strange experience to tell you. I had, as
I have told you, cut my hair in London, and I had left it piled
up in a large coil at the bottom of my trunk. One evening, after
the child was in bed, I began to amuse myself by examining the
furniture of my room and by rearranging my own little things.
There was an old chest of drawers in the room, the two upper
stages of which were empty, which I had used for my linen. These
I had filled, but below there was a wide, deep drawer, which was
locked. I had a number of keys, and I began to try whether any of
them would fit. At last, one of them did open it. The drawer
contained only one thing, but that was a very strange one. What
do you think it was, Mr. Holmes?"

"I am little of a guesser."

"It was my own hair!"

"Your own hair? But you said that you had locked it in your
trunk."

"So I did, but I took it out and looked at it. It was the same
shade and the same texture. I was quite bewildered until I took
my own hair out of my trunk and compared the two. They were
identical--a most extraordinary coincidence, was it not? I
puzzled over it for some time, but I could make nothing of it,
and so I returned the hair to the drawer and locked it up again.
Now, Mr. Holmes, I come to the part of my story of which I am
most anxious to speak.""You may have noticed, Mr. Holmes," she continued, leaning forward in her chair, "that I am not naturally a prying woman, but the atmosphere of that house would stir the curiosity of a saint. There is one particular wing, reachable only through a narrow passage off the main landing, which is guarded by a formidable door, always kept double-locked. My interest was truly ignited yesterday when I observed Toller, more heavily under the influence of drink than usual, lugging a heavy linen bag toward that very door. His movements were guarded, and the way he peered over his shoulder made it clear he wished to remain unobserved. When our eyes met, he gave a grunt of pure malice and slammed the door with such violence that the echoes rang through the house. It is that shuttered wing, Mr. Holmes, and the mystery of who or what is confined within it, that has brought me here to seek your counsel today."

"The warning was no idle one, for two nights later I happened to
look out of my bedroom window about two o'clock in the morning.
It was a beautiful moonlight night, and the lawn in front of the
house was as bright as day. I was amazed to see a terrific brute
as big as a young calf, with a huge jaw and a mane like a lion,
which was slowly passing over the grass and looking up at my
windows. It moved with a long, moaning sound which was far more
terrible than a bark. I confessed that I was chilled with fear,
and I was glad to feel that I was safely locked within my room.

"And now I have another strange experience to tell you. I had
lost my way among the passages of the house, and I found myself
in a wing which was quite new to me. At the end of a long
corridor I came to a heavy door which was locked. I was turning
away when I saw a key in the lock. I turned it and opened the
door. Inside was a small room, and at the end of it was a second
door, also locked, but this time there was no key. The room was
entirely empty, but it was strange to see that the window was
heavily barred, and that there was a strong iron shutter which
could be screwed across it from the outside. What could be the
meaning of this? As I stood wondering, I heard a step in the
passage, and the next moment Mr. Rucastle appeared. His face was
flushed with anger, and he looked at me with a most terrible
expression.

"'What are you doing here?' he asked.

"'I am afraid I have lost my way,' I stammered.

"'Then don't lose it again,' he cried, and he took me by the arm
and led me back to my own part of the house. I could see that he
was shaken with passion, and for some time after he would hardly
speak to me."That was not the only thing which made me feel that there was something very dark and strange going on in that house. One day I happened to find a small key lying upon the floor of the sitting-room. It occurred to me that it might belong to the locked drawer in my own bureau which I had been unable to open. I tried it, and the drawer sprang open. Inside there was nothing but a tress of hair. I took it out and examined it. It was of a very peculiar tint of chestnut—the exact shade of my own. I held it up against my own hair, and the two were identical. I cannot tell you how it startled me to find this, for I had been told that my hair was of a very unusual color. It seemed as though I were being made to play a part in some drama of which I knew nothing, and that my very appearance was being used for some purpose which I could not fathom."

"The warning was no idle one, for two nights later I happened to
look out of my bedroom window about two o'clock in the morning.
It was a beautiful moonlight night, and the lawn in front of the
house was silvered over and almost as bright as day. I was
standing, rapt in the peaceful beauty of the scene, when I was
aware that something was moving under the shadow of the copper
beeches. As it emerged into the moonshine I saw what it was. It
was a giant dog, as large as a calf, tawny tinted, with hanging
jowl, black muzzle, and huge projecting bones. It walked slowly
across the lawn and vanished into the shadow upon the other side.
That dreadful sentinel sent a chill to my heart which I do not
think that any burglar could have done.

"I took it up and examined it. It was of the same peculiar tint, and the same abundance. At first I thought that I must have left my own hair there, but then I remembered that I had placed it at the bottom of my trunk. I hurried to the corner of the room and pulled out the coil which I had brought from London. I held the two together. They were identical—the same extraordinary shade of chestnut. I felt a cold hand sink into my heart as I looked at them. Who was this girl who had been in the house before me, and whose hair had been shorn even as mine had been? I replaced the coil, locked the drawer, and did not say a word to anyone about my discovery, but I was more than ever convinced that some dark mystery lay behind the smiling face of Mr. Jephro Rucastle."

"I took it up and examined it. It was the same peculiar tint, and the same abundance. But then I remembered that I had my own hair safely in my trunk. I hurried to the side of the room and pulled out the contents of the box. There was my coil, as I had laid it away. I held the two in my hands, and I tell you they were identical. Was it not extraordinary? I could not explain it. I replaced the two coils and locked the drawer again, for I felt that I was on the verge of some mystery which I could not solve."

"Yes, it was my own hair, in the very same knot which I had made
before I left London. I am not superstitious, but I felt my hair
almost rise on my head at the sight of it. I had forgotten that
it was in my trunk, so I did not believe that I was looking at
anything that I could not account for. But I felt that it was a
sign of some very strange business, and that it was not by chance
that my hair had been found in that drawer. It was not in the
least likely that Mr. or Mrs. Rucastle could have taken it
themselves, and yet how could any of the others have known of its
existence?"

"You are quite sure that it was your hair?"

"I was not sure at first, but I went back to my trunk and I found
that mine was gone."

"Well, that is very remarkable," said Holmes. "And what did you
do?"

"I said nothing, but I began to think."

"The color, the texture, and even the very length of the strands
was exactly like mine. I stood and stared at it in amazement for
several minutes. It was almost as though I were looking at
myself. I cannot imagine why it was there, or what it could be.
I feel that it must have some meaning, and yet I cannot conceive
what it is. I have not been into that drawer since, but I could
not keep it from you."

"Is there any more?" asked Holmes.

"Only one more point, and I have done."

"Pray continue."

"I am coming now to the most extraordinary thing of all."

"Mr. Holmes, you can imagine my surprise when I found my own
tresses in this drawer. It was not until I had taken them out and
examined them that I realized that they were not mine. They were
exactly of the same shade, and of the same length, but they were
not mine. What did it mean? I began to realize that some
extraordinary mystery was in progress. I had been asked to wear
another person's dress, to sit in another person's place, and I
had found this person's hair in the very room which I was
occupying. I could not sleep for thinking of it. Who was this
woman, and what had become of her? I felt more and more sure that
I was filling the place of another person, and that this other
person must have been some relation to the family. Could it be
Alice, the daughter who had gone to Philadelphia? But then what
had become of her? Why had her hair been cut off? It was all very
mystifying.

"The next day I determined to explore the house, but I soon found
that my movements were watched. I had been told that there was no
one in the wing where my rooms were, and yet I was sure that I
had heard someone moving in the next room to mine. I determined
to make sure. One day, when the Rucastles were out and Toller was
as usual in the garden, I went to the door of the room which
adjoined mine. It was locked. I tried the key which had opened
the drawer, but it would not fit. I then went to the room at the
other end of the corridor, and to my surprise found that it was
also locked. I was turning away when I heard a low, moaning sound
proceeding from within. I stood for a moment, my heart beating
wildly, and then I heard a voice, very low and weak, crying, 'Is
anyone there?' I fled back to my own room, and I had hardly
reached it when I heard the heavy tread of Toller on the stairs.
He had come up to bring me my lunch, and I felt sure that he had
seen me in the corridor. He said nothing, however, and I ate my
lunch in silence.

"That afternoon I was sitting in the nursery with little Edward
when I heard a loud cry from the direction of the forbidden wing.
I ran to the door, but it was locked. I then remembered that
there was a small window in the corridor which overlooked the
roof of the wing. I ran to it and looked out. To my horror, I saw
a man standing upon the roof, his face turned towards the window
of the room where I had heard the voice. He was a small man, with
a black beard, and I recognized him at once as the man whom I had
seen in the Southampton Road. He was trying to open the window,
but it was evidently fastened from within. I was about to call
out to him when I saw Toller appearing round the corner of the
house with a large dog on a leash. The man on the roof saw him
too, for he disappeared at once, and a moment later I heard the
sound of a heavy fall. Toller ran towards the spot, and I saw him
stooping over something on the ground. I was too frightened to
stay any longer, and I ran back to the nursery.

"That evening I told Mr. Rucastle what I had seen. He seemed very
much disturbed, and he told me that I must have been mistaken.
He said that the man on the road was a common tramp, and that he
had probably been trying to break into the house. As to the voice
I had heard, he said that it was only the wind in the chimneys.
I did not believe him, but I said nothing. I felt that I was
in some danger, and that I must get help. That is why I sent you
the telegram."

"I took it up and examined it. It was of the same peculiar tint,
and the same thickness. But then the impossibility of the thing
obtruded itself upon me. How could my hair have been locked in
the drawer? With trembling hands I undid my trunk, turned out the
contents, and drew from the bottom my own hair. I laid the two
tresses together, and I assure you that they were identical. Was
it not extraordinary? Puzzle as I would, I could make nothing at
all of what it meant. I returned the strange hair to the drawer,
and I said nothing of the matter to the Rucastles as I felt that
I had put myself in the wrong by opening a drawer which they had
locked.

"I confess that I was much frightened, and yet I was at the same
time much intrigued. My thoughts were already in a very excited
state, for I could see that there was some mystery in the house,
and that my hair and my position were in some way connected with
it. I determined at last to solve it if I could. One day, a few
days later, I had a chance which I did not lose. I saw Mr. and
Mrs. Rucastle walking in the grounds together, and I found the
door which had previously been locked was now unfastened. The
keys had been left in the lock. I knew that I was doing wrong,
and that I was running a risk, but I could not resist the
temptation. I entered the room and looked about me. It was empty,
but there was a large bed in the corner, and on the wall hung a
portrait of a young woman who bore a most extraordinary
resemblance to myself. I was still looking at it when I heard a
step in the corridor and Mr. Rucastle entered. He was white with
passion, and his eyes were blazing. He did not speak a word, but
he pointed to the door. I left the room at once, but I had seen
what I wanted to see. That woman in the portrait was the
daughter who was said to have gone to Philadelphia."

"And that is all you have to tell us?" asked Holmes.

"That is all, Mr. Holmes, but I feel that there is some great
danger hanging over me, and that I am in the midst of some dark
mystery. What do you think of it all?"

"I think that you have done very well, Miss Hunter, and that you
have a very clear and a very level head. It seems to me that the
situation is a very simple one, and that the explanation of the
mystery is at our hand. I shall be ready to come down with you
to the Copper Beeches this evening if you will allow me to do
so."

"Indeed I should be very glad."

"Then we shall be there. Watson, you will come also?"

"Certainly."

"Then let us lose no time."

"This aroused my curiosity; so when I went out for a walk in the
grounds with my charge, I went round to the side from which I
could see the windows of this part of the house. There were four
of them in a row, three of which were simply dirty, while the
fourth was shuttered up. They were evidently all deserted. As I
strolled along, however, glancing up at them, Mr. Rucastle
stepped out from the hall door. He was his sunny, guffawing self
once more.

"'Ah,' said he, 'you must not think me rude if I passed you
without a word, my dear young lady. I was deeply engaged with
business matters.'

"I assured him that I was not offended. 'By the way,' said I,
'you seem to have quite a suite of spare rooms up there, and one
of them has the shutters up.'

"He looked at me with what seemed to me to be a suspicious
glance.

"'Photography is my hobby,' said he. 'I have made my darkroom up
there. But, dear me! what an observant young lady we have got!
Pray, who would ever have dreamed that you would have noticed the
shutter?'

"He spoke in a jesting tone, but there was no jest in his eyes as
he looked at me. I read suspicion there and a menace, but I gave
no sign of it. I had reached my limit of endurance, however, and
I determined to leave the house at the first possible
opportunity. That is why I sent you the telegram, and I have only
this afternoon to wait until your train arrives and I can get
your advice."

"You have done quite right," said Holmes, "and the case is a
singularly interesting one. I have already formed my own
conclusions, but I should like to ask you one or two questions
before I act upon them. You say that you have never seen anyone
in that locked wing?"

"Never."

"And you have no idea what is in it?"

"None at all."

"Have you ever heard any sounds from it?"

"I have thought that I heard a low moaning once or twice, but it
might have been the wind in the trees."

"Quite so. And now, about the servants. You say Toller is often
drunk?"

"Yes, and he was very far gone this morning. I believe he is
sleeping it off now."

"And his wife?"

"She is a strange, silent woman, but I have seen her carrying a
tray of food towards that locked door."

"That is very suggestive. Now, Miss Hunter, I should like to
come to the Copper Beeches this evening. Could you manage to let
us in?"

"I think so. The Rucastles are going out to dinner."

"Excellent. Then we shall be there at seven o'clock."

This set my curiosity into a flame. I felt that there was something evil in this house, and I was determined to get to the bottom of it. My opportunity came yesterday. Toller, the groom, had been drinking heavily, and he had left the key in the door of the forbidden wing. I waited until I saw Mr. Rucastle go out for his walk, and then I slipped up the stairs and turned the key in the lock. The passage beyond was short and ended in a heavy, iron-clamped door. As I approached it, I was startled to hear the sound of someone moving within the room, and then a low, deep sigh, as of a person in the last extremity of despair. I was about to knock, when the thought of the mastiff and of Mr. Rucastle's face came back to me, and I fled back to my own room, trembling in every limb.

"This piqued my curiosity, Mr. Holmes, and I determined to see
what was behind that door. My opportunity came this morning
when I found the key had been left in the lock. I slipped in and
found myself in a short passage with a door at the end. This
door was locked from the outside, but there was a slit in the
paneling through which I could see into the room beyond. It was
dark, but as my eyes became accustomed to the gloom, I saw that
it was furnished as a bedroom. What startled me most, however,
was to see a woman's shadow pass across the light of a shuttered
window. I was about to cry out when I heard a heavy step behind
me, and there was Mr. Rucastle. He looked at me with a face so
distorted by rage that I shrank back against the wall. He did
not strike me, but he spoke in a whisper that was more
terrifying than a shout, telling me that if I ever dared to look
into that room again, he would throw me to the mastiff."

"This aroused my curiosity; so when I went out for a walk in the
grounds with my charge, I took some pains to examine the windows
of this part of the house. There were four of them in a row,
three of which were simply dirty, while the fourth was shuttered
up. They all looked like the windows of ordinary bedrooms. As I
stood surveying them and wondering what might be inside, Mr.
Rucastle came out to me. He was as jolly and as merry as ever.

"'Ah!' said he, 'you are looking at that wing of the house, Miss
Hunter. It is as lonely as it looks, is it not?'

"'It does seem rather unoccupied,' said I.

"'The fact is,' said he, 'that I keep my photographic apparatus
in there. I am a great enthusiast in photography, and I have
made my dark-room up there. But, dear me! what a secretive
creature you are! To think of your being a trained detective and
never telling me of it! You want to know what is in those rooms,
now, don't you?'

"'I confess that I should like to know.'

"'Well, you shall know. Look through here.' He took a small key
from his pocket and opened the door. We passed into a dark
passage and through another door into a very large room. There
was nothing in it whatever but some empty boxes and a large pile
of old newspapers. It was certainly very commonplace and very
innocent.

"But just as we were turning to go out I noticed that in one
corner there was a small wooden door which was fastened by a
stout bar on the outside.

"'And what is there?' I asked.

"'Only the water-tank,' said he. 'We have no cistern, and so we
are obliged to have a tank in the roof.'

"As he spoke he drew the bar, and I saw that the door opened
into a dark, narrow space which seemed to lead into the very
heart of the house. I had no doubt that it was the tank room,
and yet there was something in the way in which he had barred the
door and in the look which he gave me as he did so which made me
feel that he was not telling me the whole truth. But I have not
long to stay now, and I must hurry back. I shall be at the Copper
Beeches at three o'clock. Tell me, Mr. Holmes, what does it all
mean, and what should I do?"

perform one more feat? I should not ask it of you if I did not
think you a quite exceptional woman."

"I will try. What is it?"

"Excellent!" cried Holmes. "You are indeed a woman after my own
heart. We shall be at the gate at seven, and you will be there to
meet us. You have your revolver, Watson? It is as well. There is
a spirit of evil in this house, and one which may be manifested
in a very practical form. We shall be with you, then, at seven."

"Excellent!" Holmes looked at his watch. "It is now half-past one. If you leave at once you will be back in time. We shall spend the afternoon in exploring the neighbourhood of the Copper Beeches, and we shall be at the hall door at seven. Goodbye, then, and be of good courage." We watched her out of the room, and then Holmes turned to me with a look of grim satisfaction. "What do you make of it, Watson?" he asked.

"Excellent!" said Holmes. "We shall then have a clear field. It is a very pretty case, and I think that I can see the end of it. You were brought down to personate some person, and that person is, of course, Miss Alice Rucastle, who was said to have gone to America. You were chosen because of your resemblance to her, and the hair was sacrificed and the dress worn in order to carry out the deception. The man in the road was her lover, no doubt, and it was necessary to show him that she was happy and well, and that her mind was quite changed towards him. But that girl is a prisoner in that chamber, and it is our task to set her free. You will be ready for us at seven, then, and we shall not fail you."

"I should be glad if you would take my friend and myself with
you. We shall not be long. We shall leave you here for an hour or
two, and then we shall walk over to the Copper Beeches, so as to
arrive there by seven o'clock."

"It shall be as you wish."

"I have no doubt at all as to what this mystery means, Miss
Hunter. The woman in the room is the daughter Alice, who has
never been to Philadelphia at all, and whom it is the object of
these people to keep from the man who is watching from the
road."

"Is that your opinion?"

"It is my conviction. And why they have used you as they have is
now equally clear to me. They have a daughter who resembles you
closely in figure and in the colour of her hair. They have made
you wear her dress and sit in her window, so as to make this
man, her lover, believe that she is still there and that she is
not being ill-treated. Then they would make you wave him away so
as to make him believe that she did not care for him. He would
see you laughing and talking with her father, and he would come
to the conclusion that he had been mistaken, and that she was
perfectly happy and contented. The reason why they have made you
cut your hair is, of course, because theirs was cut, probably
during a fever. Then they have made you wear the dress, and sit
in the window, and read, and laugh, and all the rest of it. It is
all a plot, and a very clumsy one, too."

"But why should they wish to keep her a prisoner?"

"Ah, there comes the question. Probably there is some money
matter. I have no doubt that they have been trying to make her
sign away some of her property, and that her refusal is the cause
of her imprisonment. That is what we must find out when we go to
the Copper Beeches to-night."

"I must have a little more information, Miss Hunter. You say that
you have seen Toller go into that wing with a black bag?"

"Yes."

"And you have heard sounds within?"

"Yes."

"Then there is someone there. Who it is I cannot say. We must
ascertain it, and that soon. Your safety, Miss Hunter, is my
first consideration."

"Oh, thank you, Mr. Holmes."

"But do you not think that it is very extraordinary? Mr.
Rucastle's daughter Alice is in Philadelphia, is she not?"

"Yes."

"Then who is in that room?"

"I cannot tell."

"Well, we shall see."

"Good-bye, then, Mr. Holmes, and I shall expect you at the Copper
Beeches at seven o'clock."

"I shall be there."

"Excellent! We shall then look thoroughly into the affair. Of
course there is only one feasible explanation. You have been
brought there to personate someone, and the real person is
imprisoned in this chamber. That is obvious. As to who this
prisoner is, I have no doubt that it is the daughter, Miss Alice
Rucastle, if I remember right, who was said to have gone to
America. You were chosen, doubtless, as resembling her in height,
figure, and the colour of your hair. Hers had been cut off, very
possibly in some illness through which she has passed, and so, of
course, yours had to be sacrificed also. By a curious chance you
came upon her tresses. The man in the road was undoubtedly some
friend of hers--possibly her fiancé--and no doubt, as you wore
the girl's dress and were so like her, he was convinced from your
laughter, whenever he saw you, and afterwards from your gesture,
that Miss Rucastle was perfectly happy, and that she no longer
desired his attentions. The dog is let loose at night to prevent
him from endeavouring to communicate with her. So much is fairly
clear. The most serious point in the case is the disposition of
the child."

"What on earth has that to do with it?" I ejaculated.

"I am sure that you are right, Mr. Holmes!" cried our client. "A
thousand thanks for your advice. I shall go back and do as you
suggest."

"We shall be there at seven o'clock," said Holmes, as he opened
the door for her.

"Well, Watson, what do you think of it?" he asked, as she was
shown out.

"A very pretty little case, and one which would have pleased
Inspector Lestrade."

"I should think so. I have little doubt that we shall find the
poor girl imprisoned in that chamber. And when we have liberated
her, then we shall see whether there is anything which the law
can do."

"I am sure that it is as you say. But who could be the true
culprit in such a case? It seems that they are all in it."

"No doubt, no doubt. But we shall see. There is Toller, who seems
to be the most active agent. And Mrs. Toller, who is as much in
it as her husband. And the Rucastles, who are at the bottom of
it. But there is one who is more guilty than the rest. We shall
soon find out who it is."

"I hope so," said I. "But it is a very dark and mysterious
business."

"Well, let us get our lunch and then we shall start."

"I am sure that you are right, Mr. Holmes!" cried Miss Hunter.
"I feel that you have hit upon the truth. I can see it all now.
How could I have been so blind? I will do my part, and you may
rely upon me. But what can we do when we get there?"

"That we must leave to the circumstances," answered my friend.
"But now, Miss Hunter, you must hasten back, for your absence may
already have been noted."

She rose and held out her hand to each of us. "Good-bye, then,
Mr. Holmes, and good-bye, Dr. Watson. I shall expect you at seven
o'clock at the Copper Beeches."

With a quick, firm step she was gone, and we were left alone.

"I am sure that you are right, Mr. Holmes!" cried Miss Hunter.
"I feel that you have hit it. But what can be their object?"

"Ah, that is where we are at fault. But we shall see. You must
get back now. If you should find Toller and his wife at the house
on your return, you must make some excuse for getting her into
the cellar, and then you will let us in. Be sure to have the door
open when we come. Good-bye! We shall be at the Copper Beeches at
seven o'clock."

"One moment," said I. "There is one point which you have not
cleared up. What was the meaning of the mirror?"

"Ah, that is simple. He wished her to see what was behind her,
and yet not to appear to be looking. The mirror was merely a
means to that end. But now we must be moving. Good-bye, Miss
Hunter, and do not fail us."

We saw her off by the three o'clock train, and then returned to
our hotel, where we spent the next few hours in a state of
expectant excitement. Punctually at half-past six we started for
the Copper Beeches, and by seven o'clock we were at the gates of
the park. It was a large, square house, with the clumps of copper
beeches from which it took its name, and we could see the windows
of the inhabited rooms glowing with light. Everything was still
around, and we made our way to the front door, which stood open.
Miss Hunter was waiting for us in the hall.

"Have you managed it?" asked Holmes.

"Yes. Mrs. Toller is in the cellar, and I have the key in my
pocket. Her husband is in a state of stertorous insensibility
upon the kitchen floor. He has been drinking all day. Mr. and
Mrs. Rucastle went off in their carriage about an hour ago."

"Then the coast is clear. Now for the mystery of the empty
wing."

We followed her up the stairs to the locked door, which she
opened with the key which she had taken from Toller's pocket. In
a moment we were in the passage, and stood before the barricaded
door. Holmes drew a knife from his pocket and cut the cords which
fastened the iron bar. Then he turned the key in the lock, and
the door swung open. To our surprise, the room was empty. There
was a bed, a chair, and a table, but of the prisoner there was no
sign. The skylight above was open, and it was evident that she
had made her escape.

"Someone has been before us!" cried Holmes. "We are too late!"

At that moment we heard the sound of wheels upon the gravel
outside.

"It is the Rucastles!" cried Miss Hunter. "They have returned!"

"Quick! into the room!" said Holmes. "We must not be seen."

We had hardly closed the door when we heard the sound of heavy
footsteps in the passage. Then the door was burst open, and Mr.
Rucastle stood before us. His face was purple with passion, and
he glared at us with the eyes of a madman.

"What is the meaning of this?" he cried. "What are you doing in
my house? And where is my daughter?"

"Your daughter has escaped, Mr. Rucastle," said Holmes, stepping
forward. "And as to what we are doing here, we are here to
protect this young lady from your violence."

"Protect her! I'll protect her!" he screamed, and he rushed at
Holmes with his fists clenched.

But at that moment a loud, piercing shriek rang through the
house. It was followed by the sound of a heavy fall and then by a
succession of deep, guttural groans.

"The dog!" cried Miss Hunter. "Someone has let the dog loose!"

Mr. Rucastle turned as white as a sheet. "Carlo!" he gasped.
"He's loose! He'll kill her!"

He rushed out of the room and down the stairs, and we followed
him as fast as we could. When we reached the hall, a ghastly
sight met our eyes. The great mastiff was crouching over a prostrate
figure, its fangs buried in the throat. Mr. Rucastle rushed at
the dog and tried to pull it away, but it turned upon him with a
savage growl, and he fell back, bleeding from a dozen wounds.

"Help! help!" he shrieked. "He's killing me!"

Holmes and I rushed forward, and with the help of a heavy stick
which I had brought with me, we succeeded in beating off the dog.
The creature slunk away into the darkness, and we turned our
attention to the victim. It was Mrs. Rucastle. She was quite
dead. Her throat had been torn open, and she must have died
almost instantly.

Mr. Rucastle was also badly hurt, but he was still conscious. He
moaned with pain as we lifted him up and carried him into the
drawing-room.

"It was her," he whispered. "It was her all the time. She
hated Alice, and she wanted her money. She was the one who
imprisoned her, and she was the one who let the dog loose to-night.
She thought it was Alice who was escaping, and she wanted the
dog to kill her. But he turned on her instead. It was her own
fault--her own fault."

He closed his eyes and sank into a state of unconsciousness.

"A strange ending to a strange case," said Holmes, as we stood
looking down at the wounded man. "It seems that we have been
mistaken, Watson. It was not the father, but the stepmother, who
was the villain of the piece. Her jealousy and her greed have led
to this terrible tragedy."

"And what of Miss Alice Rucastle?" I asked.

"She has no doubt escaped with her lover," said Holmes. "We
shall probably hear from them before long. But for the present,
our work here is done."

And so it proved. Miss Alice Rucastle had indeed escaped with her
fiancé, Mr. Fowler, who had been the man in the road. They were
married shortly afterwards, and they lead a happy and prosperous
life. As for Mr. Rucastle, he recovered from his wounds, but he
was a broken man, and he never again showed any of the joviality
which had been his most marked characteristic. The Copper
Beeches was sold, and the memory of the terrible events which had
taken place there gradually faded away.

"It has been a most interesting case, Watson," said Holmes, as
we sat together in our room at Baker Street a few weeks later.
"One of those cases which show how much more extraordinary life
is than anything which the imagination can invent. And yet, if
you had not been there to help me, I do not know how it would
have ended."

"I am glad to have been of service," I replied. "But I think
that the real credit belongs to Miss Violet Hunter. Her courage
and her intelligence were the real factors in the case."

"Quite so," said Holmes. "She is a most remarkable woman. I
should not be surprised if we heard more of her in the future."

But we never did. She became the head of a private school at
Walsall, where she met with considerable success. And so the case
of the Copper Beeches came to an end.

"I am sure that you are right, Mr. Holmes!" cried Miss Hunter.
"And I should be so happy if I could help to rescue her. But now
I must go, or I shall be late. I will do as you have told me."

"We shall be at the gate at seven," said Holmes, as he conducted
her to the door. "But before we go I will call at the house of a
detective whom I know in Winchester, for it may be as well to
have an officer of the law with us."

"That is a good idea," said I. "I shall look forward with the
greatest interest to our next visit."

"And so shall I," said Holmes. "I am sure that we shall find
plenty to occupy us."

"I am sure you are right, Mr. Holmes!" cried our client. "A more
unnatural child I have never seen. But what is to be done?"

"There is only one thing to be done. We must go to the Copper
Beeches and see for ourselves. Miss Hunter, you must return at
once. You must wait for us there. At seven we shall be with you.
But stay! What if the Rucastles do not go?"

"I think that they will. They have ordered the dog-cart to be
ready for them. I will return at once, then, and I will do as you
have told me."

"Then good-bye for the present. We shall meet at seven."

"Good-bye." And she hurried off towards the station.

"That's a girl of some character, Watson," said Holmes, as we sat
together over our lunch.

"Indeed she is. And what are we to do now?"

"We must get down to Winchester as soon as possible. There is a
train at 4:15. We shall just be in time."

"Then we had better be moving."

"In one moment. I want to look up one thing." He turned to a
thick volume which lay upon a side-table. "Ah, here it is. 'Lord
Southerton's preserves. Two miles from the station of
Sparsholt.' That is where we must go."

"Why?"

"Because we should find it more convenient to approach the house
from the back. I have no doubt that it is perfectly safe, but we
cannot be too careful. Now, Watson, if you are ready."

"I am sure that you are right, Mr. Holmes," cried our client. "A
thousand things come back to me which make me certain that you
have hit it. Oh, let us lose not an instant in bringing help to
this poor creature."

"We must be circumspect, for we are dealing with a very cunning
man. We can do nothing until seven o'clock. At that hour we shall
be with you, and it will not be long before we solve the
mystery."

"Yes, Mrs. Toller is safe in the wine-cellar, and her husband
lying in a state of hopeless intoxication in the kitchen. Here
are the keys of the house. I will lead the way."

"We must not lose a moment," said Holmes, as we followed her up
the stairs. "I am sure that there is some villainy going on
there. The man is a scoundrel, and if we are not quick we may be
too late."

"But what could he do?" I asked.

"He could kill her, for all we know to the contrary. He is a
desperate man, and he will go to any length if he is driven to
extremity. Now, Miss Hunter, this is the door, I believe."

"Yes, it is."

"And the key is not here?"

"No, I should think it is with Mr. Rucastle."

"Then we must break it in."

He set his shoulder against the door, and with a crash it flew
open. We found ourselves in a small, dark passage, with three
doors in a line, the middle one being the one which we sought.
It was, as Miss Hunter had described it, strongly barricaded with
the iron bar. Holmes at once began to undo the fastenings, but as
he did so he suddenly stopped and looked at the floor.

"Good heavens!" he cried. "We are too late."

"What is it?" I asked, looking over his shoulder.

"Look at this! Blood!"

He pointed to a small, dark pool which lay just outside the
door, and which was still wet and glistening.

"It has come from under the door," said he, and as he spoke he
threw himself against the heavy woodwork. With a loud crash the
door gave way and we found ourselves in the room beyond. It was,
as Miss Hunter had said, lighted from a skylight, but the room
was empty. There was no one there.

"She is gone!" cried Holmes. "We are too late."

"But where can she have gone?" I asked.

"Into the next world, I fear," said Holmes, and his face was
very grave. "Wait! What is this?"

He stooped and picked up a small, dark object from the floor. It
was a lady's glove, and it was soaked with blood.

"There has been foul play here," said he, "and I fear that we
shall never see the poor girl alive again. But who can have done
this thing? Not Mr. Rucastle, for he has been away all the
evening."

"But Toller and his wife?" I suggested.

"Toller was too drunk to have done it," said Miss Hunter, "and
his wife was in the cellar."

"Then there must be someone else in the house," said Holmes.
"But who can it be?"

As he spoke there was a loud cry from downstairs, followed by
the sound of a struggle. We rushed down the stairs and into the
hall, where we found a man struggling with a woman. The man was
Mr. Rucastle, and the woman was Mrs. Toller.

"What is the meaning of this?" cried Holmes, as he stepped
between them.

"The meaning of it is that this woman has murdered my daughter!"
cried Mr. Rucastle, his face distorted with passion. "I found
her just now in the hall with my daughter's glove in her hand,
and she has confessed that she killed her and threw her body into
the woods."

"It's a lie!" cried Mrs. Toller, her face pale with terror. "I
never killed her. It was she who did it!" and she pointed to
Mrs. Rucastle, who was standing in the doorway, her face as white
as a sheet.

"You lie, you jade!" cried Mr. Rucastle, and he made a rush at
her, but Holmes caught him by the arm and held him back.

"Wait a moment, Mr. Rucastle," said he. "There is some mystery
here which must be cleared up. Watson, keep an eye on these two
women, while I have a word with Mr. Rucastle."

He led the way into the dining-room, and we followed him,
leaving Miss Hunter and the two women in the hall.

"Now, Mr. Rucastle," said Holmes, when we were alone, "what is
the meaning of this extraordinary story?"

"It is simple enough," said Mr. Rucastle, who had recovered his
composure to some extent. "My daughter Alice was a source of
great trouble to me. She was headstrong and self-willed, and she
insisted upon marrying a man of whom I did not approve. I
forbade the marriage, and she then became so violent that I was
obliged to confine her to her room. I hoped that in time she
would see the folly of her ways, but she remained obstinate.
This evening, when I returned from my visit, I found that she had
been murdered by Mrs. Toller, who had always hated her. She has
confessed the crime, as I told you."

"And where is the body?" asked Holmes.

"She says that she threw it into the woods."

"And where is Mrs. Rucastle?"

"She is in the hall, as you saw."

"And she also accuses Mrs. Toller?"

"Yes."

"It is a very strange story," said Holmes, "and I should like to
hear what Mrs. Toller has to say for herself."

He went to the door and called the woman in.

"Now, Mrs. Toller," said he, "what have you to say to this
charge?"

"It's a lie, sir, a wicked lie!" cried the woman, bursting into
tears. "I never touched the poor girl. It was Mrs. Rucastle who
did it. She has hated her ever since she came to the house, and
she was always egging her husband on to be cruel to her. This
evening, when they were away, she came back unexpectedly and
found that I had left the door of the room open. She went in and
killed the poor girl with a knife, and then she made me help her
to carry the body into the woods. She said that if I didn't she
would tell her husband that it was I who had done it, and he
would kill me. I was so frightened that I did what she told me,
but I never touched the girl myself."

"And where is the body now?" asked Holmes.

"It's in the woods, sir, near the copper beeches."

"And the knife?"

"Mrs. Rucastle has it, sir. She hid it in her room."

"This is a very serious charge, Mrs. Rucastle," said Holmes,
turning to the lady, who had entered the room while Mrs. Toller
was speaking. "What have you to say to it?"

Mrs. Rucastle did not answer. She stood with her eyes fixed upon
the floor, her face as pale as death.

"I think that we had better go and look for the body," said
Holmes. "Watson, you stay here with Mr. Rucastle and Miss Hunter,
while I go with Mrs. Toller and Mrs. Rucastle."

He led the way out of the room, and we heard their footsteps
dying away in the distance.

"This is a most terrible business," said Mr. Rucastle, sinking
into a chair and burying his face in his hands. "To think that my
own wife should have done such a thing! I can hardly believe it."

"It is indeed a terrible business," I said, "but we must wait and
see what Mr. Holmes discovers."

We sat in silence for some time, the only sound being the ticking
of the clock upon the mantelpiece. At last we heard footsteps
returning, and Holmes entered the room, followed by Mrs. Toller.
He was very pale, and his face was set and stern.

"Well?" I asked. "Have you found the body?"

"No," said Holmes, "we have not found the body, for there is no
body to find."

"What do you mean?" cried Mr. Rucastle, starting up from his
chair.

"I mean that your daughter is alive and well, Mr. Rucastle," said
Holmes, "and that this whole story of her murder was a cruel and
wicked plot on your part to get rid of your wife."

"To get rid of my wife!" cried Mr. Rucastle. "What do you mean?"

"I mean that you have long been tired of your wife, and that you
wished to marry again. You knew that your daughter's presence in
the house was a constant reminder of your first wife, and you
determined to get rid of her. You confined her to her room and
treated her with the greatest cruelty, in the hope that she would
die. But she was strong and she lived on. Then you hit upon this
diabolical plan. You knew that Mrs. Toller was a weak and
frightened woman, and you easily persuaded her to join you in
your plot. You smeared the floor with blood, and you placed the
soaked glove in the hall, to make it appear that a murder had
been committed. You then accused Mrs. Toller of the crime,
knowing that she would in turn accuse your wife. You hoped that
your wife would be convicted of the murder and that you would
thus be free to marry again. It was a clever plot, Mr. Rucastle,
but you forgot one thing."

"And what was that?" asked Mr. Rucastle, his face livid with
rage.

"You forgot that I was in the house," said Holmes, "and that I
am not easily deceived. I saw through your plot from the first,
and I have now found your daughter, who is safe and sound in the
care of her fiancé, Mr. Fowler. He has been waiting for her in
the woods, and they are now on their way to Winchester, where
they will be married to-morrow."

"You have ruined me!" cried Mr. Rucastle, and he made a rush at
Holmes, but I stepped between them and held him back.

"It is you who have ruined yourself, Mr. Rucastle," said Holmes,
"by your own wickedness and cruelty. You will now have to answer
to the law for your treatment of your daughter, and for your
dastardly attempt to incriminate your wife. Watson, I think that
we have done all that we can here. Miss Hunter, I shall be happy
to escort you back to Winchester."

And so we left the Copper Beeches, with its dark and sinister
secrets, and drove back to the old city, where we saw Miss Hunter
safely into her train. As for Mr. Rucastle, he was arrested and
sentenced to a long term of imprisonment, while his wife, who
had been so cruelly wronged, eventually found happiness in a new
life. And so ended the adventure of the Copper Beeches, one of
the most singular and interesting cases that ever came under the
notice of Mr. Sherlock Holmes.

"I have done my part, Mr. Holmes. Mrs. Toller is in the cellar,
and I have the key in my pocket. Toller is in a state of
insensibility in his own room."

"Capital! capital! Then we have only to take our friend with us
and see what she has to say."

"Wait!" I cried. "There is one other person to be accounted for.
Where is the boy?"

"The child is with his nurse in the garden. I have seen to that."

"Then let us proceed at once."

We were soon at the foot of the stair, and followed Miss Hunter
to the first-floor landing. We had but a moment to pause before
the door, and then we had entered the deserted wing. All was
exactly as Miss Hunter had described it. We walked down the long,
bare passage and found the central door, with its iron bar and
its padlock.

"This is the door!" said Miss Hunter.

Holmes drew his revolver and examined it with some care.

"I see no other way," said he, "but to use force."

"One moment!" I cried. "Let me try my strength first."

I put my shoulder to the door, and with a mighty effort I burst it
open. The room within was small and bare, with a single skylight
above. A small bed stood in one corner, and there were a few
pieces of furniture about. But there was no sign of a prisoner.
The room was empty!

"Yes. I told Mrs. Toller that she should go to the wine-cellar
and fetch some wine for Mr. Rucastle, and then I turned the key
upon her. She is there now, and she must be very much surprised
at being treated in such a fashion."

"And where is the man, Toller?"

"He is in his little room, I believe, and quite unconscious. He
has been drinking since midday, and I have just seen him, fast
asleep. I think that we may consider ourselves quite safe for
the evening."

"That is well. Let us proceed at once."

We went into the hall, and Holmes led the way to the stair, Miss
Hunter close at his heels, and I following after. We crossed the
silent house, until we reached the corridor which led to the
empty wing. The door stood open, and we passed through. There
before us was the barricaded door of which we had heard so much.
With a heavy blow of his heel Holmes broke through the thin wood,
the padlock gave way, and the door was open. We rushed into the
room, but it was empty. There was nothing there but a bed, a
broken chair, and a table with some books upon it. The skylight
above was open, and the prisoner, whoever she had been, had fled.

"There has been some villainy here," said Holmes. "Someone has
been before us."

"But who could it be?" asked Miss Hunter.

"I cannot imagine. But here is the man, Rucastle, coming up the
stairs. We shall soon know."

We heard the heavy tread of a man's feet, and then the door of
the wing was thrown open, and the master of the house appeared.
He was a very different-looking man to the jovial,
smiling person whom we had seen in London. His face was distorted
with rage, and his small eyes were gleaming with a tigerish
light.

"So," he cried, "you have been into my house, have you? You have
been into my private rooms! You have been meddling with things
which do not concern you!"

"I am Sherlock Holmes," said my friend, stepping forward. "I am
here at the request of Miss Hunter to see that justice is done."

"Justice!" cried Rucastle, with a harsh, discordant laugh. "I'll
give you justice! I'll give you more than you bargained for!"
He turned and rushed from the room.

"He's gone for the dog!" cried Miss Hunter.

"Quick! We must stop him!" shouted Holmes, and we all rushed
down the stairs and out into the garden.

We were only just in time. Rucastle was at the door of the
outhouse, and was just in the act of slipping the bolt. As he did
so the huge brute within gave a low, deep growl, and then, with a
snarl which made my blood run cold, it sprang out and at its
master's throat. Rucastle fell back with a cry of agony, and the
great dog, its fangs buried in his neck, bore him to the ground.
I rushed forward and fired my revolver into the animal's brain,
and it fell dead beside its victim.

We carried the unfortunate man into the house, and I did what I
could for his injuries, which were very severe. It was evident,
however, that he was in no immediate danger of his life.

"And now," said Holmes, as we stood together in the hall, "we
must find out what has become of the lady. But first we must
release Mrs. Toller."

He went to the cellar door and turned the key. Mrs. Toller
emerged, looking very much ashamed of herself.

"Now, Mrs. Toller," said Holmes, "we want to know what has
become of Miss Alice Rucastle."

The woman looked from one to the other of us in a bewildered
fashion.

"I don't know what you mean," she said at last. "I don't know
anything about Miss Alice Rucastle."

"Come, come!" said Holmes. "It is useless to deny it. We know
that she was imprisoned in that room. We want to know where she
is now."

"I tell you I don't know," the woman repeated. "I have never
seen her since she went away to Philadelphia."

"This is very strange," said Holmes. "But I think that I begin
to see light. Watson, would you be so good as to go and see how
the man Toller is getting on?"

I went to the room where the groom was lying, and found him still
in a heavy, drunken sleep. I returned and reported this to
Holmes.

"Then it was not he," said he. "Mrs. Toller, you are a very
faithful servant, no doubt, but I think that you would be wise
to tell us the truth. Your master is very seriously injured, and
it may be that he will not recover. It would be better for you to
tell us all that you know."

The woman's face changed as she heard this, and she looked at us
with a more communicative expression.

"I'll tell you all I know," she said. "It wasn't my doing, and I
always told Mr. Rucastle that no good would come of it. Miss Alice
was a very good young lady, and it was a shame to treat her so.
She was in love with a gentleman of the name of Fowler, but her
father wouldn't hear of it. He wanted her to marry someone else,
someone with money, I believe. And when she wouldn't do it, he
shut her up in that room and told everyone that she had gone to
America. He even made me write letters for her, and send them to
be posted in Philadelphia, so that people might think she was
there."

"And what has become of her now?"

"She's gone away with Mr. Fowler. He came for her this evening,
while the master and mistress were out. He had a ladder, and he
got her out through the skylight. I saw them go, but I didn't
say anything, for I was glad to see her get away."

"I see," said Holmes. "And now there is one more thing. Who was
it that put the hair in the drawer in Miss Hunter's room?"

"That was Mrs. Rucastle," said the woman. "She found it in the
room where Miss Alice had been, and she thought that it would be
a good thing to have it in case it was needed."

"I think that we have now the whole story," said Holmes. "And
it is a very pretty one, in its way. Mr. Rucastle has been
severely punished for his wickedness, and I think that we may
leave him to the care of his wife and the doctor. Miss Hunter, I
congratulate you upon the part which you have played in this
matter. You have shown yourself to be a very brave and capable
woman."

And so ended the adventure of the Copper Beeches. Mr. Rucastle
recovered from his injuries, but he was always a broken man, and
his wife and the Tollers remained with him to the end. Miss Alice
Rucastle married Mr. Fowler and lived happily ever after, while
Miss Hunter became the head of a private school at Walsall, where
she met with considerable success.

"Mrs. Toller is in the cellar, and I have the key in my pocket.
As to Toller, he is at this moment lying in a drunken sleep upon
the kitchen table. He will be as quiet as a dead man."

"Then let us lose no more time."

"Is the house empty?" asked Holmes.

"Quite. Except for the child, who is asleep."

"Then to the empty wing at once."

Miss Hunter led the way up the stairs and down the long corridor,
until we reached the door which led into the deserted part of the
house. It was unlocked, and she pushed it open. Following her, we
quickly found ourselves in the little passage where she had
received so severe a fright. At the end of it was the barricaded
door.

"This is the room," said she. "I am sure of it."

"Then we will have it open in a trice."

Holmes took a large key from his pocket and applied it to the
lock, but it would not turn.

"It is a peculiar lock," said he. "I must try another."

He tried a second and a third, but with no better result.

"Is there no other way of entering?" I asked.

"There is the skylight," said Miss Hunter.

"But it is very high up, and we have no ladder."

"There is a small trap-door in the roof above the landing. I saw
it yesterday when I was exploring."

"That will do! That will do!" cried Holmes, and he hurried back
to the landing.

"But we must be quick," said Miss Hunter. "The Rucastles may be
back at any moment."

"I will be as quick as I can," said Holmes, as he clambered up on
to a chair and thence on to the trap-door. "Now, Watson, your
hand! So! Now, Miss Hunter! One more effort and we are there."

In another minute we were all three standing upon the roof of the
Copper Beeches. It was a large, flat, leaden-covered space,
interrupted here and there by the chimneys and the skylights.

"This must be it," said Holmes, pointing to a small,
square-paned window which was let into the roof. "And, look! it
is open!"

He hurried towards it and looked down.

"Empty!" he cried. "The bird has flown!"

"Empty!" I ejaculated.

"Empty!" cried Miss Hunter. "But I heard someone in there only
yesterday."

"Then they must have moved her," said Holmes. "But where? and
why? Ah, I have it! Rucastle must have suspected that his secret
was discovered, and he has taken her away. But how? and where?
Watson, look round! Is there no trace? No clue?"

I looked round the roof, but there was nothing to be seen but the
leaden surface and the chimneys.

"Stay!" cried Holmes. "What is this?"

He stooped down and picked up a small, dark object which was
lying near the skylight.

"A button!" he cried. "A large, black, bone button! And, look!
it has been torn from a coat, for there is a piece of the cloth
still attached to it."

"But what does it mean?" I asked.

"It means that there has been a struggle," said Holmes
thoughtfully. "And a struggle which has taken place very
recently, for the cloth is quite fresh. Now, who could have been
struggling here? And why? Ah, I have it! Toller! It was Toller!
He was the only person who could have had access to this room.
And he has been drinking, you say, Miss Hunter?"

"Yes, he has been drinking very heavily lately."

"Then that explains it! In his drunken frenzy he has attacked
the poor girl and has carried her away. But where? Where could he
have taken her?"

"Wait!" I cried. "I hear someone coming!"

We all listened intently. From below there came the sound of
heavy, stumbling footsteps, and then a loud, drunken voice
calling out:

"Mrs. Toller! Mrs. Toller! Where are you, you jade? Where have
you got to?"

"It is Toller himself!" whispered Miss Hunter. "He must have
woken up!"

"Then we have him!" cried Holmes. "Follow me! Quick!"

He hurried to the trap-door and scrambled down, followed by Miss
Hunter and myself. As we reached the landing we saw a tall,
burly man, with a red, bloated face and bloodshot eyes,
staggering towards us. In his hand he held a large, heavy
kitchen poker.

"So!" he cried, as he saw us. "It's you, is it? You've been
prying into things that don't concern you, have you? Well, I'll
teach you to mind your own business!"

He raised the poker and rushed at Holmes, but my friend was too
quick for him. With a sudden movement he tripped the drunken man
up, and he fell heavily to the floor, the poker clattering away
from him.

"Now, Watson! The cord! Quick!" cried Holmes.

I whipped a piece of cord from my pocket and in another minute
we had the fellow securely bound hand and foot.

"Now, then," said Holmes, as he stood over his prostrate foe.
"Where is Miss Alice Rucastle? What have you done with her?"

The man only glared at him with his bloodshot eyes and muttered
an oath.

"It is no use," said Holmes. "He is too drunk to speak. But we
must find the girl. Search the house, Watson! Search every room!
She must be here somewhere!"

I hurried away to carry out his instructions, but though I
searched every room in the house, from the attic to the cellar,
I could find no trace of the missing girl. When I returned to
the landing I found Holmes and Miss Hunter still standing over
the bound man.

"Have you found her?" asked Holmes.

"No. She is not in the house."

"Then where can she be? Ah, I have it! The outhouse! The
outhouse where the dog is kept! It is the only place we have not
searched!"

We all hurried down the stairs and out into the grounds. As we
approached the outhouse we heard a low, moaning sound coming
from within.

"It is she!" cried Miss Hunter. "It is Miss Rucastle!"

Holmes hurried to the door and tried to open it, but it was
locked.

"The key!" he cried. "Where is the key?"

"I have it here," said a voice behind us.

We all turned round to see Mrs. Toller standing there, a grim
smile upon her face.

"So you've found her, have you?" she said. "Well, it's about
time someone did. My husband's a brute when he's in drink, and
he's been treating that poor girl shamefully."

She handed the key to Holmes, who quickly unlocked the door and
entered the outhouse. In another minute he emerged, carrying a
slight, pale-faced girl in his arms. She was unconscious, and her
face was covered with bruises.

"She is alive!" cried Holmes. "But she has been cruelly
treated. Watson, your brandy-flask! Quick!"

I handed him the flask, and after a few sips of the spirit the
girl began to revive. She looked round her with a dazed
expression, and then, as her eyes fell upon Mrs. Toller, she
shrank back with a cry of terror.

"Don't be afraid, Miss Rucastle," said Holmes kindly. "You are
safe now. We are your friends, and we have come to rescue you."

"But where is he?" she whispered. "Where is Mr. Rucastle?"

"He is away for the evening," said Holmes. "But we have your
father's servant, Toller, safely bound. It was he who attacked
you, was it not?"

"No, no!" cried the girl. "It was not Toller! It was my father!
It was Mr. Rucastle himself!"

"Your father!" I ejaculated.

"Yes. He has been keeping me a prisoner in that room for months,
because I would not sign away my property to him. And to-night,
when he found that you were coming, he tried to kill me! He
dragged me out here and was going to throw me to the dog, but
Toller interfered. They had a struggle on the roof, and Toller
managed to get me away and hide me in here. But my father is
coming back! He will be here at any moment! Oh, save me! Save
me!"

"Do not fear, Miss Rucastle," said Holmes. "You are safe with
us. And as for your father, I think we shall be able to deal with
him when he arrives."

Even as he spoke, the sound of wheels was heard upon the gravel
drive, and a minute later a dog-cart drew up at the front door.
Mr. Rucastle jumped out and hurried into the house, followed by
his wife.

"Where is she?" we heard him cry. "Where is that girl? Toller!
Toller! Where are you?"

He came rushing out into the grounds, his face purple with rage.
As he saw us he stopped short, and a look of terror came into
his eyes.

"So!" he cried. "It's you, is it? The meddling detective and his
friend! Well, you're too late! She's gone! I've sent her away
where you'll never find her!"

"On the contrary, Mr. Rucastle," said Holmes calmly. "Miss
Rucastle is here, and she has told us everything."

"It's a lie!" cried Rucastle. "A wicked, malicious lie! She's
mad! I tell you, she's mad!"

"I think not," said Holmes. "And as for your conduct, I think
the law will have something to say to that. Watson, I think we
had better take Miss Rucastle to Winchester at once. We can
leave Mr. Rucastle to the care of the police."

And so it was that the mystery of the Copper Beeches was solved,
and the wicked plot of Jephro Rucastle was brought to light. Miss
Rucastle was restored to her friends and her property, and her
father was brought to justice for his crimes. As for Toller, he
was severely reprimanded for his part in the affair, but as he
had ultimately saved Miss Rucastle's life, he was allowed to go
free. And so ended one of the most singular and interesting
cases that ever came under the notice of Mr. Sherlock Holmes.

"Mrs. Toller is in the cellar. I have turned the key upon her.
The master and mistress are gone, and Toller is, I think, quite
helpless. Oh, come in at once! My heart is in my mouth until I
know that that poor girl is safe."

"Lead the way, Miss Hunter," said Holmes, as he followed her up
the stairs.

"Wait a moment!" I cried. "I thought I saw a face at that window
in the wing which you said was deserted."

"Impossible! No one is there but the prisoner."

"Indeed I saw it--a pale, anxious face, looking out for a
moment."

"Well, let us see, let us see!" Holmes hurried forward, and in a
few seconds we were at the door of the empty rooms. He turned the
key, and we found ourselves in the passage. The central door was
still barred and padlocked.

"It is too late!" cried Miss Hunter. "She is gone! The bar is
down, and the door is open!"

"What does it mean?" I asked.

"It means that she has been warned, and that she has escaped."

"Or that she has been moved," said Holmes. "Well, let us see for
ourselves." He stepped into the room and then came out again with
