a very grave face. "This is very serious," said he. "The
skylight is open, and she has evidently climbed out upon the
roof. It would be no easy task for a woman, but a desperate woman
would do it."

"She would not be alone, then," I suggested.

"No, no, she would have a helper. But who? Some one must have
known of our coming."

"I told no one," cried Miss Hunter.

"Nor I," said I.

"Stay!" cried Holmes. "What is this?"

He stooped down to the floor and picked up a small, crumpled
piece of paper. It was a note, written in a hurried, trembling
hand.

"Help! help! I am being taken away. They have discovered all.
Alice."

"They have discovered all!" cried Holmes. "Then they must have
known that we were coming. But how?"

"Look!" I cried, pointing to the window. "There is Mr. Rucastle
driving up the road."

"And he is alone," said Holmes. "If he has the girl with him, she
must be in the back of the dog-cart. But no, he is alone. Where
can he have taken her?"

"He is coming to the house!" cried Miss Hunter. "He will find us
here!"

"Let him come," said Holmes. "We have the law on our side. But we
must be quick. Watson, keep your eye on the door. Miss Hunter,
stay here. I must see if I can find any clue as to where they
have taken her."

He began to search the room with his usual energy, but in a few
moments we heard the sound of wheels on the gravel outside, and
then the heavy tread of a man on the stairs. The door was flung
open, and Mr. Rucastle stood before us. His face was purple with
rage, and his eyes were flashing.

"So!" he cried. "This is how you repay my kindness! You bring
these men here to spy upon me! You shall repent it, I tell you!
You shall repent it!"

"Mr. Rucastle," said Holmes, "we are here to find Miss Alice
Rucastle. We know that she has been imprisoned in this room, and
we mean to find out where she is now."

"You do, do you?" cried Rucastle, with a hideous grin. "Then you
shall find her in a way you little expect! Toller! Toller! set
the dog loose! Set the dog loose, I say!"

He turned and rushed down the stairs, and we heard him shouting
for the groom.

"The dog!" cried Miss Hunter. "He will set the dog on us!"

"We must get out of this!" cried Holmes. "Quick, Watson, the
window! It is our only chance!"

He hurried to the window and threw it open. It was a long drop to
the ground, but there was a thick growth of ivy which might
support us. Holmes swung himself out, and I followed him, with
Miss Hunter close behind. We reached the ground in safety, just
as we heard the baying of the hound and the sound of Rucastle's
voice cheering him on.

"This way!" cried Holmes, and we ran towards the gate. But we
were too late. The great hound was already upon us, his eyes
glowing like coals and his jaws dripping with foam. He sprang at
Holmes, but my friend was ready for him. He struck him a heavy
blow with his stick, and the brute fell back, howling with pain.

"Now, Watson, now!" cried Holmes, and we rushed past the dog and
out of the gate. We did not stop until we were well away from the
house, and then we sank down on the grass, breathless and
exhausted.

"Well," said Holmes, as he wiped his brow, "that was a narrow
escape. But we have not finished yet. We must find Miss Rucastle,
and we must find out who it was that warned them of our coming."

"But how can we do that?" I asked.

"There is only one person who could have known," said Holmes.
"And that person is Mrs. Toller."

"Mrs. Toller!" I cried. "But she was locked in the cellar!"

"Quite so," said Holmes. "But she might have had a confederate.
And I think I know who that confederate was."

"Who?" I asked.

"Toller," said Holmes. "He was not as drunk as he seemed. He was
playing a part, just as his master was. And it was he who warned
Rucastle of our coming."

"But why?" I asked.

"That is what we must find out," said Holmes. "And I think I see
a way to do it. Come, Watson, we must get back to the inn and see
if we can find any further information."

We made our way back to the Black Swan, where we found Miss
Hunter waiting for us. She was still very much agitated, but she
had recovered her composure somewhat.

"Oh, Mr. Holmes," she cried, "what are we to do? That poor girl!
What will become of her?"

"Do not despair, Miss Hunter," said Holmes. "We shall find her, I
promise you. But first I must ask you a few questions. Did you
see anything else in that room, anything that might give us a
clue?"

"No," said Miss Hunter. "I was so frightened that I didn't look.
But wait! I did see something. There was a small, black bag on
the floor, near the bed. I remember now."

"A black bag!" cried Holmes. "That is what Toller was carrying!
We must get that bag, Watson. It may contain the clue we are
looking for."

"But how can we get it?" I asked. "The house is guarded by that
dog."

"We must find a way," said Holmes. "And I think I know how. Miss
Hunter, can you get back into the house without being seen?"

"I think so," she said. "There is a small side-door which is
usually left unlocked."

"Good," said Holmes. "Then you must go back and get that bag. We
will wait for you here."

"But the dog!" she cried.

"Do not worry about the dog," said Holmes. "I have a plan for
him. Just get the bag and bring it to us as quickly as you can."

Miss Hunter hesitated for a moment, and then she nodded. "I will
do it," she said. "For the sake of that poor girl, I will do it."

She hurried away, and Holmes and I waited in the sitting-room of
the inn. It seemed like hours before she returned, but at last we
heard her step on the stairs. She was breathless and pale, but
she was carrying the black bag.

"I have it!" she cried, as she sank into a chair. "I have it!"

Holmes took the bag and opened it. Inside were a few pieces of
paper, a small key, and a photograph. He looked at the photograph
first. It was of a young woman, very like Miss Hunter, but with
a sadder, more weary expression.

"Miss Alice Rucastle," said Holmes. "And these papers? Let us see
what they are."

He began to read the papers, his brow furrowing as he did so. "As
I thought," he said at last. "It is a conspiracy. A conspiracy
to rob this poor girl of her inheritance."

"Rob her of her inheritance!" I cried. "But how?"

"It is a long story," said Holmes. "But the gist of it is this:
Miss Rucastle's mother left her a large sum of money, which was
to come to her on her marriage. Her father, Jephro Rucastle, was
determined to get his hands on that money, and he hit upon this
plan to do it. He imprisoned his daughter, and then he hired
Miss Hunter to personate her, in the hope that her fiancé would
be deceived and would give up his claim to her hand. In that way,
Rucastle would be able to keep the money for himself."

"But what about the Tollers?" I asked. "What part did they play
in it?"

"They were his accomplices," said Holmes. "They were paid to keep
watch over the girl and to help him in his scheme. But it seems
that they were not entirely satisfied with their share of the
spoils. They wanted more, and they were willing to betray their
master to get it."

"But who was the true culprit?" I asked. "Who was the one who
planned it all?"

"That is the question," said Holmes. "And I think I have the
answer. Look at this note again."

He held up the piece of paper he had found in the room. "Help!
help! I am being taken away. They have discovered all. Alice."

"What of it?" I asked.

"Look at the handwriting," said Holmes. "It is not the same as
the handwriting in the letters which Miss Rucastle wrote to her
fiancé. It is a much more forceful, more determined hand. And it
is the same hand as the handwriting in this note."

He held up another piece of paper, which he had taken from the
black bag. It was a short note, addressed to Mr. Rucastle.

"We must be careful," it said. "The girl is getting suspicious.
We must move her at once. Mrs. Toller."

"Mrs. Toller!" I cried. "Then she was the one who planned it
all!"

"Exactly," said Holmes. "She was the brains behind the whole
affair. Rucastle was merely a tool in her hands. She was the one
who saw the opportunity to rob the girl, and she was the one who
devised the plan to do it. She was the true culprit."

"But where is Miss Rucastle now?" I asked.

"She is safe," said Holmes. "I have already sent a telegram to
the police, and they are on their way to the Copper Beeches. They
will find the girl and they will arrest the Rucastles and the
Tollers. Our work is done."

"And Miss Hunter?" I asked.

"Miss Hunter has shown herself to be a woman of great courage and
resource," said Holmes. "I have no doubt that she will find a
much better situation than the one she has just left. And as for
us, Watson, I think we have earned a good night's rest."

And so ended the adventure of the Copper Beeches. It was one of
the most singular cases in my friend's career, and one which
showed, perhaps more than any other, the power of his remarkable
faculties of deduction and analysis.

A loud thudding noise came from somewhere downstairs. "That is
Mrs. Toller in the cellar," said she. "Her husband lies snoring
on the kitchen rug. Here are his keys, which are the duplicates
of Mr. Rucastle's."

"You have done well indeed!" cried Holmes with enthusiasm. "Now
lead the way, and we shall soon see the end of this black
business."

The door was strong, and it resisted our combined efforts, but at
last we felt it yield, and with a sudden crash it flew open. The
room was a large one, but it was empty. It was quite a pretty
room, with its walls covered with a flowery paper, and its soft,
dainty-coloured carpet. A single bed, a chair, and a wardrobe
formed the furniture. A skylight above admitted a glimmer of
dying day, and we could see that a small round table with a
flower-glass on it was at the side of the bed. Everything was
neatly and tastefully arranged, and showed that whoever had been
living there had been treated with care and consideration.

"Where is she? Where can she have gone?" cried Miss Hunter.

Holmes looked around him with a clouded brow. "It is my belief
that we have come too late," said he. "They have spirited her
away. But how? See that skylight! It is big enough for a man to
pass through."

"I think that there is something more in this than meets the
eye," I remarked. "Does it not strike you as being a very well
furnished and comfortable prison?"

"It is most extraordinary," said Holmes. "But look! What is
that?"

He pointed to a small, dark object which was lying on the floor
near the bed. I picked it up. It was a small, heavy, metal box.
Holmes took it from my hand and examined it.

"It is locked," said he. "We must find a way of opening it."

He took a small, sharp instrument from his pocket and in a few
moments the box was open. It was filled with papers, but on the
top lay a small, folded note. Holmes opened it and read it
aloud.

"'To whom it may concern: I, Alice Rucastle, being of sound mind
and body, do hereby declare that I am leaving the Copper Beeches
of my own free will. I am going to join the man I love, and I
implore my father and stepmother to forgive me for the step I am
taking. I can no longer endure the life of a prisoner, even
though my prison be a gilded one. Alice Rucastle.'"

"This is most extraordinary," said Holmes, as he finished reading
the note. "It seems that our prisoner has escaped of her own
accord."

"But how could she have done it?" asked Miss Hunter. "The door
was locked and barred, and the skylight is far too high for her
to reach."

"That is the question," said Holmes, "and it is one which I
intend to answer. But first, let us see if we can find any other
clues in this room."

He began to search the room thoroughly, examining every nook and
cranny. Suddenly, he stopped and looked at the floor near the
wardrobe.

"Look here, Watson!" he cried. "What do you make of this?"

I looked where he was pointing and saw a small, dark stain on the
carpet. It was about the size of a crown piece and looked like
dried blood.

"It is blood!" I exclaimed.

"Yes," said Holmes, "and it is fresh. It cannot have been there
for more than a few hours. This puts a very different complexion
on the matter. It seems that our prisoner did not escape as
easily as she would have us believe."

"But where is she now?" asked Miss Hunter, her face pale with
fear.

"That is what we must find out," said Holmes. "But first, let us
see if we can find any other traces of her."

He continued his search, but there was nothing more to be found.
The room was as silent as a grave.

"We must go downstairs," said Holmes at last. "Perhaps we can
find some clue there. And we must also have a word with Mrs.
Toller. She may know more than she is willing to admit."

We left the room and hurried downstairs. As we reached the
bottom of the stairs, we heard the sound of a carriage driving up
to the door.

"It is the Rucastles!" cried Miss Hunter. "They have returned!"

"Quick!" said Holmes. "We must hide!"

We ducked into a small room off the hall and waited. A few
moments later, we heard the front door open and the sound of
voices.

"Where is Miss Hunter?" we heard Mr. Rucastle ask.

"I do not know, sir," replied Mrs. Toller's voice. "I have not
seen her for some time."

"Well, find her at once!" said Mr. Rucastle. "I have something
important to tell her."

We heard Mrs. Toller's footsteps receding as she went in search
of Miss Hunter.

"Now is our chance," whispered Holmes. "Follow me!"

He led the way out of the room and towards the back of the house.
We passed through the kitchen, where Toller was still snoring on
the rug, and out into the garden.

"Where are we going?" I asked.

"To the mastiff's kennel," said Holmes. "I have a suspicion that
we may find something there."

We reached the kennel and Holmes looked inside. It was empty.

"The dog is gone!" he exclaimed.

"But where could he have gone?" I asked.

"That is what we must find out," said Holmes. "But look! What is
that?"

He pointed to a trail of blood which led from the kennel towards
the woods.

"It is the same blood as we saw in the room!" I cried.

"Yes," said Holmes, "and it is leading us straight to the
culprit."

We followed the trail of blood into the woods. It was dark and
the trees were thick, but we managed to keep on the trail.
Suddenly, we heard a low, growling sound.

"It's the dog!" whispered Miss Hunter.

We crept forward cautiously and saw the mastiff standing over a
prostrate figure. It was Mr. Rucastle! He was lying on the ground,
his clothes torn and his face covered in blood. The dog was
snarling and snapping at him, and it was clear that he was in
great danger.

"Help! Help!" he cried, as he saw us.

Holmes rushed forward and grabbed the dog by the collar. He was
a strong man, but it took all his strength to hold the savage
creature back.

"Watson, help me!" he cried.

I rushed to his side and together we managed to pull the dog away
from Mr. Rucastle.

"Are you all right, sir?" I asked, as I helped him to his feet.

"Yes, yes, I think so," he gasped. "But the dog... he went mad!
He attacked me!"

"It seems that your 'beauty' has turned against you, Mr.
Rucastle," said Holmes, his eyes flashing with anger. "But where
is your daughter? Where is Alice Rucastle?"

Mr. Rucastle looked at him with a startled expression. "Alice?
She is in Philadelphia," he stammered.

"No, she is not," said Holmes. "She was a prisoner in that room
upstairs, and she has escaped. And it was you who tried to stop
her, was it not?"

Mr. Rucastle looked down at the ground and said nothing.

"It is all over, Mr. Rucastle," said Holmes. "We know
everything. We know how you tried to force your daughter to sign
away her inheritance, and how you imprisoned her when she
refused. We know how you hired Miss Hunter to personate her, in
order to deceive her fiancé. And we know how you tried to kill
her when she escaped."

"No, no, it was not me!" cried Mr. Rucastle. "It was... it was
Toller!"

"Toller?" said Holmes. "And why would Toller want to kill your
daughter?"

"He... he was in love with her," stammered Mr. Rucastle. "He
wanted her for himself. And when she refused him, he went mad
with rage. He was the one who imprisoned her, and he was the one
who tried to kill her."

"A likely story," said Holmes. "But we shall see what the police
have to say about it."

He turned to me. "Watson, go and find the police. And tell them
to bring a carriage. We have a prisoner to transport."

I did as I was told and soon the police arrived. They took Mr.
Rucastle into custody, and we all went back to the house.

As we were leaving, we saw Mrs. Toller standing in the doorway.
She was looking at us with a strange expression on her face.

"So, you have found out the truth at last," she said.

"Yes," said Holmes, "we have. And it seems that your husband was
not the only one involved in this black business."

Mrs. Toller looked at him for a moment and then turned away.

"You will never find her," she said, as she walked away. "She is
gone, and you will never find her."

"We shall see about that," said Holmes.

We left the Copper Beeches and drove back to Winchester. It had
been a long and difficult day, but we had at last solved the
mystery of the Copper Beeches.

But as we were sitting in the train on our way back to London,
Holmes looked at me with a serious expression.

"There is one thing which still bothers me, Watson," he said.

"And what is that?" I asked.

"The blood," he said. "The blood in the room, and the blood on
the trail. It was not the blood of a human being. It was the
blood of a dog."

"A dog?" I exclaimed.

"Yes," said Holmes. "And it was not the blood of the mastiff.
It was the blood of another dog. A smaller dog. A dog like the
one that Mr. Rucastle's son was so fond of killing."

"You mean... the child?" I gasped.

"Yes," said Holmes. "It was the child who killed the dog. And
it was the child who helped Alice Rucastle to escape."

"But why?" I asked.

"Because he loved her," said Holmes. "She was the only one who
was ever kind to him. and he could not bear to see her a
prisoner. And so he killed the mastiff, and he helped her to
escape through the skylight. And then he wrote that note, in
order to protect her."

"It is a strange and terrible story," I said.

"Yes," said Holmes, "it is. But it is also a story of love and
sacrifice. And it is a story which I shall never forget."

And so ended the adventure of the Copper Beeches. Alice Rucastle
was never found, but it was said that she had gone to join her
fiancé in America, and that they were living happily ever after.
As for Mr. Rucastle, he was sentenced to a long term of
imprisonment, and his wife and son were left to live out their
days in the lonely house among the copper beeches. And as for
Sherlock Holmes, he returned to his rooms in Baker Street, ready
to take on the next challenge that came his way.

With a loud crack the door gave way, and we were inside the
room. It was empty. The floor was uncarpeted and the walls were
without paper. Not even a chair or a table was to be seen in the
apartment, and yet there was a something which showed that it had
been inhabited. Not a thing had been left behind. Not even a
morsel of food or a drop of water. But on the floor was a small
and dirty-looking bundle. Holmes hurried towards it and picked it
up.

"A girl's dress!" he cried. "The same shade of blue! But where
is the girl?"

"And who has taken her?" I asked.

"Ask not who but where, Watson," said Holmes, with his brows
knit and a look of deep concern upon his face. "If she were here
and had been moved, where would she have been taken to? It is a
vast house, and there are many hiding-places."

"Could it be that her father has taken her away?"

"No, for he is not yet returned. This must have been done within
the last few hours."

"By whom?"

"By the Tollers, I should imagine. They are the only people who
have been in the house."

"But they were both drunk?"

"So it was said, but let us see."

"Wait!" cried Miss Hunter, from the doorway. "Listen!"

A loud and piercing scream Rang through the house. It was a woman's 
voice, and it was filled with such a sound of terror and of 
agony as I have never heard before.

"It is Mrs. Rucastle!" cried Miss Hunter. "She is in the 
kitchen!"

We rushed down the stairs as fast as our legs could carry us. As 
we reached the kitchen we saw a sight which I shall never 
forget. Mrs. Rucastle was lying upon the floor, her face buried 
in her hands, and she was sobbing and moaning in a heart-rending 
fashion. Beside her stood her husband, his face pale and his 
eyes flashing with anger.

"What is the meaning of this?" he cried, as we entered the 
room. "What are you doing here?"

"We are here to help Miss Rucastle," said Holmes, in a stern 
voice. "Where is she?"

"She is gone," said Rucastle, with a sneer. "She has escaped."

"Escaped? How?"

"She was let out by those two drunken fools, the Tollers. I have 
just found them in the cellar, and they have confessed everything."

"Confessed everything? What do you mean?"

"They have confessed that they were bribed by that fellow in the 
road to let her go. They have been in league with him all along. 
It was they who told him when she would be at the window, and it 
was they who helped her to escape this afternoon."

"But how could they have done it?" I asked. "They were both 
drunk."

"Drunk? They were no more drunk than I am. It was all a trick to 
deceive me. They have been plotting this for weeks, and now they 
have succeeded."

"And where is she now?" asked Holmes.

"She is with him, I suppose. They have gone off together."

"And what about the dog?" I asked. "How did they get past him?"

"The dog? They must have drugged him. I found him lying in his 
kennel, as still as a stone."

"But why should they have done this?" I asked. "What interest 
had they in her escape?"

"Money, I suppose. That fellow in the road must have paid them 
well. But they shall pay for it, I can tell you that. I'll have 
the law on them, if it's the last thing I do."

"I think that you will find that the law has something to say to 
you, Mr. Rucastle," said Holmes, in a cold and level voice. "You 
have been guilty of a very serious crime in imprisoning your 
daughter in this fashion."

"A crime? It was for her own good. She was not herself. She was 
suffering from a mental derangement, and it was necessary to 
keep her under restraint."

"That is a matter for the doctors to decide, not for you. And 
what about Miss Hunter? Why did you bring her here and make her 
personate your daughter?"

"That was my wife's idea," said Rucastle, with a glance at his 
sobbing wife. "She thought that if the fellow in the road saw 
someone who looked like Alice, he would be convinced that she 
was happy and well, and that he would go away and leave us in 
peace."

"And you were willing to sacrifice Miss Hunter's hair and her 
peace of mind for such a purpose?"

"She was well paid for it," said Rucastle, with a shrug of his 
shoulders. "She knew what she was doing when she accepted the 
situation."

"I think that you will find that the law takes a very different 
view of the matter," said Holmes. "In the meantime, we must find 
Miss Rucastle and her friend."

"You will never find them," said Rucastle, with a triumphant 
grin. "They have had a good start, and they are far away by 
now."

"We shall see about that," said Holmes. "Watson, will you stay 
here and keep an eye on these people? I shall go to the police 
station and give the alarm."

"I will stay," I said.

Holmes hurried from the room, and I was left alone with the 
Rucastles and Miss Hunter. Mrs. Rucastle was still sobbing 
upon the floor, and her husband was pacing up and down the 
room, his face filled with rage and defiance. Miss Hunter was 
standing by the window, her face pale and her eyes filled with 
tears.

"It is a bad business," she said, in a low voice. "A very bad 
business."

"It is indeed," I said. "But we must hope for the best."

"The best? What can be the best in such a case as this?"

I did not answer, for I did not know what to say. We waited in 
silence for what seemed like an eternity, until at last we 
heard the sound of wheels upon the drive. It was Holmes, 
returning with a party of police.

"We have them!" he cried, as he entered the room. "We have 
found them both!"

"Where?" I asked.

"At the station. They were just about to board a train for 
London. They are both in custody now."

"And Miss Rucastle?"

"She is safe. She is with the police matron at the station. 
She is very weak and exhausted, but she is out of danger."

"And the man?"

"He is a Mr. Fowler, a very respectable young man, it seems. 
He has been in love with Miss Rucastle for some time, but her 
father would not hear of the match. He has been trying to 
rescue her ever since she was imprisoned."

"And the Tollers?"

"They are also in custody. They have confessed everything. 
It seems that they were indeed bribed by Mr. Fowler to help 
Miss Rucastle to escape."

"And what about the dog?"

"The dog was indeed drugged, as Mr. Rucastle suspected. It was 
Mrs. Toller who did it. She has a great deal of influence with 
the animal, it seems."

"And what will happen to the Rucastles?"

"They will be charged with kidnapping and false imprisonment," 
said Holmes. "It is a very serious offence, and they are 
likely to receive a heavy sentence."

"I am glad of it," said Miss Hunter. "They deserve everything 
that they get."

"And what about you, Miss Hunter?" I asked. "What will you do 
now?"

"I shall go back to London," she said. "I have had enough of 
the country to last me for a lifetime."

"I don't blame you," I said. "It has been a very trying 
experience for you."

"It has indeed. But I am glad that I was able to help."

"You have been very brave," said Holmes, with a smile. "You 
have done a great service to Miss Rucastle and to the cause of 
justice."

"Thank you, Mr. Holmes. I am glad that you think so."

And so the case of the Copper Beeches came to an end. The 
Rucastles were indeed convicted and sentenced to a long term of 
imprisonment. Miss Rucastle and Mr. Fowler were married shortly 
afterwards, and they are now living happily in London. As for 
Miss Hunter, she has found a much more congenial situation in 
the city, and she is now one of the most successful governesses 
in the country. Sherlock Holmes returned to his studies and his 
investigations, and I to my medical practice, but we both 
often think of that strange and terrible experience at the 
Copper Beeches, and of the brave young woman who helped us to 
solve the mystery.

With a loud crash the door gave way, and we burst into the room.
It was small, with a low ceiling and a skylight from which the
daylight was fast fading. The bed stood in the corner, and on it
lay a girl, but she was motionless, and her face was buried in
the pillow.

"Oh, no!" cried Miss Hunter, who had followed us into the room.
"Have they killed her? Is she dead?"

But Holmes had already his fingers on the pulse of the girl's
wrist. "She is only in a deep sleep," said he. "It is some
narcotic, I should think, for her breathing is regular, but her
face is very flushed. But look here! What is this?"

He pointed to a small glass which was standing on a table beside
the bed. It was half full of a dark fluid, and there was a
peculiar smell about it.

"Laudanum!" I exclaimed. "They have drugged her!"

"It would seem so," said Holmes. "But why? Why should they drug
her now, when she was already their prisoner? And what is this? A
note?"

He picked up a small piece of paper which was lying on the floor
beside the bed. On it was written in a hurried, trembling hand:
"My dear friend, do not be afraid. I am going away with someone
who will protect me. Forgive me for the trouble I have caused
you. Alice Rucastle."

"It's a forgery!" cried Holmes. "The handwriting is quite
different from that of the letter which Miss Hunter received.
Wait! I hear someone coming!"

He had hardly spoken when the door was flung open and a man
rushed into the room. It was Mr. Rucastle, his face distorted
with passion and his eyes flashing with a light which was almost
maniacal.

"What are you doing here?" he cried. "How dare you break into my
house! Out of this at once, or I'll set the dog on you!"

"We shall not go until we have taken this young lady with us,"
said Holmes, pointing to the girl on the bed. "Your villainy is
discovered, Mr. Rucastle."

"My villainy! What do you mean? This is my daughter, and she is
ill. I have a right to do what I like with her. Go, I tell you,
or it will be the worse for you!"

He turned and rushed out of the room, and we heard his footsteps
clattering down the stairs.

"He has gone for the dog!" cried Miss Hunter. "He will let him
loose upon us!"

"We must follow him!" said Holmes. "Watson, look after the young
lady. Miss Hunter, stay here."

He ran out of the room, and I followed him as fast as I could.
But we were too late. As we reached the hall we heard a savage
snarl and a scream of agony. We rushed out into the garden and
there we saw a sight which I shall never forget.

Mr. Rucastle was lying on the ground, and the giant mastiff had
his teeth in his throat. The man was struggling feebly, but the
dog was too strong for him.

"Down, Carlo! Down!" cried a voice, and a woman ran forward and
seized the dog by the collar. It was Mrs. Toller. She managed to
drag the dog away, and then she turned to us with a face which
was white with terror.

"Oh, my God!" she cried. "He's killed him! He's killed him!"

We ran to the fallen man, but it was too late. Mr. Rucastle was
dead. The dog had torn his throat open, and he had bled to death
in a few seconds.

"It's a judgment!" said Mrs. Toller, shaking her head. "A
judgment from heaven for all his wickedness. He's been a cruel
man to that poor girl, and now he's met his end."

"But who let the dog loose?" asked Holmes.

"I did," said Mrs. Toller. "I saw him coming out of the house
with that look on his face, and I knew what he was going to do.
He was going to set the dog on you, and I couldn't let him do
that. So I let the dog loose myself, and he went for his master
instead."

"But why did he go for his master?" I asked.

"Because he hadn't been fed for two days," said Mrs. Toller. "Mr.
Rucastle had forgotten all about him in his rage against his
daughter, and the dog was half mad with hunger. When he saw his
master he just sprang at him."

"And the daughter?" asked Holmes. "What was the meaning of that
note?"

"It was Mrs. Rucastle who wrote it," said Mrs. Toller. "She
wanted to make it look as if Miss Alice had run away of her own
accord, so that no one would suspect what had happened to her.
She's been as bad as her husband, and she's the one who's been
drugging the poor girl to keep her quiet. She's a wicked woman,
is Mrs. Rucastle."

"And the man in the road?" asked Holmes.

"That was Mr. Fowler," said Mrs. Toller. "He's been hanging about
the house for weeks, trying to get a word with Miss Alice. He's
a good man, and he wanted to marry her, but Mr. Rucastle wouldn't
hear of it. He wanted Miss Alice's money for himself, and he was
determined that she should never marry."

"It's a strange story," said Holmes, "and a dark one. But at
least the poor girl is safe now. We must see that she is taken to
a place of safety, and then we must inform the police of what has
happened."

And so ended the adventure of the Copper Beeches. Miss Alice
Rucastle recovered from the effects of the drug, and she was
eventually married to Mr. Fowler. Mrs. Rucastle and the Tollers
were all arrested, but as there was no evidence against them
they were eventually released. As for Miss Hunter, she returned
to London and resumed her career as a governess, and I have no
doubt that she is still doing well.

"It was a curious case, Watson," remarked Holmes as we sat in
the train on our way back to London. "A very curious case
indeed. And yet, as I told you, it was only by following the
logical sequence of events that we were able to arrive at the
truth. Crime is common, but logic is rare. Remember that,
Watson, and you will never go far wrong."

The door was a stout one, and I had some difficulty in forcing it
open. At last it gave way, and we burst into the room. It was
empty! There was no one there. The iron bed stood in one corner,
undone and without bedding. On the table were some bread and
water and a volume of a religious book. A skylight was open above
our heads, and through it the girl must have escaped.

"It is all clear now," said Holmes. "The girl has been spirited
away, and that through the window. But we may still be in time to
thwart her captors."

"If you're looking for the girl," a gruff voice spoke from the
doorway, "you're a bit late, as usual."

We whirled round. Standing in the passage, leaning against the
doorframe with a malicious grin, was the man Toller. He was
dishevelled, his eyes bloodshot from drink, but he held a heavy
revolver leveled steadily at us. Beside him, her face a mask of
cold fury, stood his wife.

The door was a strong one, and it required several efforts on our
part before it yielded. Then we rushed into the room, which was
cold and bare. A truckle-bed, a small table, a chair, and a box
were its only furniture. On the table stood a glass of water and
half a loaf of bread, which had evidently not been touched.

"Empty!" cried Holmes. "We are too late. The bird has flown."

"What! Could she have escaped?"

"It seems to me that she must have. She had not been there for
some time, or the bread would not have been so dry. Some one has
evidently helped her to get away. But how?"

"There is the skylight!" I cried.

"Yes, but how could she have reached it? It is at least ten feet
from the floor."

"She may have stood upon the table, and then on the chair."

"Possibly, but even then she would have had to jump at least four
feet."

"No, there was a more certain way. See!"

I pointed to a ladder which was lying in the garden and leaning
up against the wall just under the skylight.

"That ladder was not there when I was looking out from my
window," said Miss Hunter. "I could see the whole garden then."

"Well, then, she must have been helped from without. There is the
entire story. But where could she have gone?"

"Wait! I hear something!" I cried.

We stood listening. In the distance we heard the sound of wheels.

"That is Mr. Rucastle returning!" cried Miss Hunter.

"Quick, then, down with you, and get to the door. We must meet
him when he comes."

"One moment," said Holmes, "I hear something else. There is a cry
coming from the direction of the cellar."

We all three hurried down the stairs, and as we reached the
bottom of them we heard a loud scream of terror and the sound of
a heavy fall.

"It is Mrs. Toller!" cried Miss Hunter. "I believe she's got out
of the cellar!"

We rushed through the kitchen and into the yard, and there a
ghastly sight met our eyes. Mrs. Toller was lying upon the ground
with her throat torn and bleeding, and the huge mastiff, his
jaws dripping with blood, was standing over her.

"The dog! The dog!" I cried.

"He has broken loose!" shouted Holmes.

"But how could he have got loose? Toller is the only one who can
manage him."

"Then Toller must have set him free!" cried Holmes. "Where is
he?"

We looked around, but there was no sign of the groom.

"Stay!" said Holmes. "What is that?"

He pointed to the outhouse where the dog was kept. The door was
standing wide open, and inside we could see the figure of a man
lying upon the floor.

"It is Toller!" I cried. "He is dead!"

"No," said Holmes, "he is only unconscious. He has been
mercilessly beaten."

"But who could have done it?"

"We shall soon see," said Holmes. "Here is Mr. Rucastle."

The dog-cart had just driven up to the door, and Mr. Rucastle,
looking very pale and agitated, sprang out and ran towards us.

"What is the meaning of this?" he cried. "What have you been
doing here?"

"We have been trying to save Miss Rucastle," said Holmes
sternly. "But we are too late. She has escaped."

"Escaped!" cried Rucastle. "How could she have escaped? I had
her under lock and key!"

"She was helped from without," said Holmes. "And now, Mr.
Rucastle, I must ask you to come with me. There are several
matters which require explanation."

"I will go with you," said Rucastle. "But first I must see to my
wife."

He ran into the house, and we followed him. We found Mrs.
Rucastle in the drawing-room, looking very pale and frightened.

"Jephro!" she cried. "What has happened? What is the matter?"

"The girl has escaped," said Rucastle. "And these gentlemen have
been making free with my house. But where is Toller?"

"He is in the outhouse," said Holmes. "He has been badly
beaten."

"Beaten! By whom?"

"That is what we have to find out," said Holmes. "But first let
us see to Mrs. Toller."

We went back into the yard, and found that the dog had been
secured by one of the grooms from the neighbouring estate, who
had heard the screams and come to the rescue. Mrs. Toller was
still alive, but her injuries were very serious.

"We must get her to the hospital at once," said Holmes. "And
now, Mr. Rucastle, I must ask you to come with me to the police
station."

"I will go with you," said Rucastle. "But I tell you, I know
nothing of all this. I was away all the evening, and my wife was
with me."

"We shall see about that," said Holmes. "And now, Watson, I
think that we have done all that we can here for the present. We
must get back to London and see what we can find out about Miss
Alice Rucastle."

As we were leaving the house, we saw a young man standing by the
gate. He was small and bearded, and wore a grey suit.

"That is the man I saw in the road!" cried Miss Hunter.

"Wait!" said Holmes. "I must speak to him."

He went up to the young man and spoke to him for a few minutes.
Then he came back to us.

"It is as I thought," he said. "That is Mr. Fowler, Miss Alice
Rucastle's fiancé. He has been trying to rescue her for weeks,
and it was he who helped her to escape to-night. He had bribed
Toller to leave the key in the door, and then he had brought a
ladder and helped her out through the skylight. But Toller, it
seems, had repented of his bargain, or perhaps he had been too
drunk to carry it out properly, and he had tried to stop them.
In the struggle that followed, Fowler had beaten him and then
set the dog loose to cover his retreat. He did not know that Mrs.
Toller was in the yard, and he is horrified at what has
happened."

"But why did the Rucastles imprison their daughter?" I asked.

"That is a long story," said Holmes. "But I think that I can
guess the reason. Miss Alice Rucastle was entitled to a large
fortune under her mother's will, but only if she married with
her father's consent. Mr. Rucastle, who was a greedy and
unscrupulous man, had no intention of letting the money go out
of the family, and so he had imprisoned his daughter to prevent
her from marrying Fowler. He had even forced her to sign a paper
giving him control of her fortune, and it was to make sure that
she was still alive and well that he had hired Miss Hunter to
personate her."

"It was a cruel and wicked plot," I said.

"It was indeed," said Holmes. "But it has been frustrated at
last. Miss Alice Rucastle is safe with her fiancé, and Mr.
Rucastle will have to answer to the law for his crimes."

And so ended the adventure of the Copper Beeches. It was a case
which had many strange and unusual features, but it was one
which, thanks to the courage and intelligence of Miss Hunter,
was brought to a successful conclusion. Mr. Rucastle was
convicted of kidnapping and assault, and was sentenced to a long
term of imprisonment. Mrs. Rucastle, who had been a passive but
willing accomplice in her husband's crimes, was also punished,
though more lightly. As for Miss Hunter, she eventually married
a wealthy and titled gentleman, and lived happily ever after.
And Sherlock Holmes, having solved yet another mystery, returned
to his rooms in Baker Street and his chemical researches.

It was an old rickety door and gave at once before our united
strength. Together we rushed into the room. It was empty. There
was no furniture save a little pallet bed, a small table, and a
basketful of linen. The skylight above was open, and the prisoner
gone.

"There has been some villainy here," said Holmes; "this beauty
has guessed Miss Hunter's intentions and has carried his victim
off."

"But how?"

"Through the skylight. We shall soon see how he managed it." He
swung himself up onto the roof. "Ah, yes," he cried, "here's the
end of a long light ladder against the eaves. That is how he did
it."

"But it is impossible," said Miss Hunter; "the ladder was not
there when the Rucastles went away."

"It is the step of a man, and he is coming this way. Now, let us
see who our new visitor is."

The door was thrown open, and a man, his face dark with passion
and his eyes bloodshot, stood upon the threshold. It was Jephro
Rucastle himself. He saw at a glance that the room was empty and
that his victim was gone.

"Where is she?" he cried. "What have you done with her?"

"We are here to ask you that," said Holmes sternly.

"I have done with you!" cried the man, and with a roar of rage
he turned and fled from the room.

"He's going for the dog!" cried Miss Hunter.

"Quick, Watson, after him!" cried Holmes. "We must not let him
loose that monster."

We rushed down the stairs after him, but we were too late. We
could hear the sharp rattling of a chain and the savage barking
of the mastiff as it was set free. Rucastle's voice was heard
encouraging the animal.

The great dog had Rucastle by the throat and was worrying him as
though he were a rat. The man lay upon the ground, his face

few minutes without having regained consciousness.

poor girl who was the cause of all this misery."

now standing in the doorway and looking at us with an expression
of the most intense astonishment.

"Mrs. Toller!" cried Miss Hunter.

"What is the meaning of this?" she asked.

"Where is Miss Rucastle?" asked Holmes.

"She is gone," said she. "Mr. Rucastle took her away by the

"I thought as much," said Holmes. "And where has he taken her?"

"Heaven help her!" I cried, and we all rushed down the stairs

But it was too late. A loud, snarling sound came from the

sufficiently sober to let the dog loose, and it was now wreaking
its vengeance upon the man who had ill-treated it.

"Call him off! call him off!" cried Holmes.

But it was only when Toller himself came out, and after some

his life was in danger.

"And I will go for the police," said Holmes.

"But what about Miss Rucastle?" asked Miss Hunter.

"She is safe enough," said Mrs. Toller. "I helped her to escape
by the skylight, and she is now on her way to Winchester."

"You helped her!" cried Holmes.

"Yes. I have been with her since she was a child, and I could
not see her ill-treated any longer. I knew what Mr. Rucastle's
plans were, and I was determined to frustrate them."

"Yes, it was I. I have been her friend all through, and I am
glad that she is safe at last."

"And so you were the true culprit, after all," said Holmes, with

sure that Miss Hunter will be glad to have been of some service
to her friend."

Sherlock Holmes and I returned to London, well satisfied with the
result of our investigation.

Our departure from the Copper Beeches marked the conclusion of a singular business. Mr. Rucastle lingered on, though his physical and mental faculties were forever diminished by the ordeal, leaving him a mere shadow of his former boisterous self under his wife’s constant supervision. Through subsequent inquiries, I learned that Alice Rucastle and her devoted sailor were wed shortly after their escape and eventually sought their fortune abroad. The Tollers, having played their part in the girl’s liberation, accompanied the young couple into their new life. As for the courageous Miss Hunter, while Holmes’s professional admiration did not, as I had once hoped, blossom into a more tender sentiment, she found her own path to prosperity. She now presides over a well-regarded educational establishment in the Midlands, a position for which her remarkable character and firm resolve have most admirably suited her.

Mr. Rucastle, though he survived the savage attack of the mastiff, remained a broken and haunted man, lingering on in a state of permanent invalidism under the watchful, silent care of his wife. As for our client, Miss Violet Hunter, she did not return to the house of the beeches, but her remarkable qualities soon found a fitting sphere, and she is now the head of a private school at Walsall, where she has met with considerable success.
